# Summary: CT-based colon imaging (CT colonography) for colorectal cancer (CRC) screening

CT-based colon imaging, also called CT colonography (CTC) or "virtual colonoscopy," uses rapid intravenous contrast-enhanced CT combined with meticulous air-contrast insufflation to evaluate the colon and rectum as a screening test for adenomas and cancers. It is a dedicated protocolized examination designed to optimize visualization of the colorectal lumen and can be performed as an outpatient without sedation. <cite id="98ad0bb2-3">CT colonography (CTC) is a defined imaging procedure distinct from standard abdomen–pelvis CT in which there is a dedicated protocol to optimize the colorectum</cite> <cite id="7786e884-1">Computed tomography colonography (CTC) is a minimally invasive structural examination of the colon and rectum to evaluate for colorectal polyps and neoplasms, with formal performance guidelines</cite> <cite id="98ad0bb2-4">CT colonography can be performed in a few minutes and does not require sedation, allowing patients to drive to and from the procedure</cite>.

## Main advantages

- Comparable detection of advanced neoplasia in screening settings: <cite id="98ad0bb2-6">In a large randomized population screening trial, CTC and colonoscopy had similar detection rates for advanced neoplasias</cite>. <cite id="bc6adcc9-5">A meta-analysis reported CTC cancer sensitivity around 96% for lesions ≥10 mm, with specificity 79.6%–93.1%</cite>.
- Noninvasive, sedation-free outpatient exam: <cite id="98ad0bb2-4">CT colonography can be performed quickly without sedation, enabling patients to drive to and from</cite>. <cite id="7786e884-0">CTC requires a full bowel preparation similar to colonoscopy, but no sedation is required and the examination is less time-consuming</cite>. <cite id="98ad0bb2-2">CT colonography has a much lower risk of perforating the colon than conventional colonoscopy</cite>.
- High sensitivity for larger (≥10 mm) adenomatous lesions and cancers: <cite id="0abf705b-7">Compared to colonoscopy, CTC has high sensitivity for adenomas ≥10 mm, with somewhat lower sensitivity for advanced adenomas ≥6 mm</cite>. <cite id="bc6adcc9-1">A 90% sensitivity for CTC in detecting polyps ≥10 mm is consistent with improvements in health outcomes</cite>.
- Useful rescue/adjunct when endoscopy is incomplete: <cite id="7786e884-5">CTC is an effective and safe choice when an obstructing colorectal cancer prevents complete endoscopic assessment or when cecal intubation fails</cite>. <cite id="7786e884-2">CT colonography is indicated for screening individuals at average or moderate risk and for surveillance of patients with a history of colonic neoplasm</cite>.
- Broader patient appeal due to tolerability and rapidity: <cite id="7786e884-0">Although CTC requires full bowel preparation, the lack of sedation and shorter overall time make it appealing to patients</cite>. <cite id="98ad0bb2-2">Most people who undergo CTC do not experience perforation, and the procedure is generally well tolerated</cite>.
- Detection of coexisting extraluminal pathology and simultaneous cross-sectional staging: <cite id="98ad0bb2-5">CT colonography provides low-dose ionizing radiation exposure and may detect extracolonic findings, which can prompt additional testing; it is unclear whether this adds net benefit</cite>. In practice, this can streamline work-up by revealing focal mesenteric nodes or pericolic soft-tissue masses in a single exam. <cite id="98ad0bb2-5">It is unclear whether detection of extracolonic findings on CT leads to clear downstream benefit</cite>.

## Main limitations and caveats

- Radiation exposure and downstream testing risk: <cite id="98ad0bb2-5">CTC carries low-dose ionizing radiation, and extracolonic findings may trigger further invasive tests, creating uncertainty about net harm vs benefit</cite>. Patient-focused resources emphasize this tradeoff. <cite id="98ad0bb2-2">CT colonography has a much lower perforation risk than colonoscopy, but like any CT it delivers ionizing radiation</cite> <cite id="7786e884-9">Guidelines note radiation exposure and the need to balance benefits with potential harm from extracolonic findings</cite>.
- Lower sensitivity in subgroups where colonoscopy excels:
  - Small lesions (<6–10 mm): <cite id="0abf705b-0">In a randomized high-risk setting, colonoscopy detected significantly more high-risk sessile serrated polyps than CTC</cite>. <cite id="0abf705b-7">CTC sensitivity is somewhat lower for advanced adenomas ≥6 mm compared to ≥10 mm</cite>. <cite id="7786e884-8">Flat nonpolypoid lesions are challenging for radiologists, with nonpolypoid lesions ≥5 mm sometimes missed relative to colonoscopy</cite>.
  - Nonpolypoid/flat lesions and sessile serrated adenomas (SSAs): <cite id="0abf705b-4">CT colonography has high sensitivity (~95%) for CRC and polyps ≥10 mm, but sensitivity drops to 75%–80% for nonpolypoid adenomas</cite>. <cite id="0abf705b-5">Nonpolypoid lesions ≥5 mm can be seen at CTC but missed at colonoscopy in some series, highlighting differing visualization and polyp-capture limitations</cite>.
  - Overall head-to-head accuracy vs colonoscopy: <cite id="0abf705b-0">Colonoscopy shows higher detection of high-risk sessile serrated polyps than CTC in randomized comparisons</cite>. <cite id="0abf705b-6">Colonoscopy finds 98% of lesions ≥10 mm vs 59% for CTC and 48% for air–barium enema in head-to-head comparisons</cite>.
- Bowel preparation quality, pain/cramping, and operator/protocol dependence: <cite id="7786e884-0">CTC requires a full bowel preparation similar to colonoscopy, which contributes to patient burden and must be performed competently</cite>. Poor preparation can obscure lesions and raise the need for repeat testing. Dedicated protocols and experienced teams help mitigate these risks. <cite id="7786e884-1">Formal practice parameters outline technical performance standards for CTC</cite>.
- Potential for false positives and over-investigation: <cite id="98ad0bb2-2">While perforation risk is low, extraluminal nodules or incidental lesions can be seen on cross-section and are not clinically relevant, which may cause additional testing</cite> <cite id="7786e884-5">Some guidelines emphasize using CTC as one option for average-risk screening and in surveillance, reflecting the need for judicious use to avoid overdiagnosis cascades</cite>.
- Access and reimbursement constraints (varies by payer and time): <cite id="98ad0bb2-5">Historically, screening CTC was not broadly covered due to radiation and workflow concerns</cite>. <cite id="7786e884-3">Some payers exclude coverage for screening CT colonography (CPT 74263) in asymptomatic patients</cite>. However, policy is evolving: <cite id="7786e884-7">Medicare coverage for screening CTC (CPT 74263) became standard of care effective January 1, 2025, with guidance on coinsurance and MAC implementation</cite>. <cite id="7786e86977-4">CMS' Multisociety/CMS evidence review acknowledges screening CTC as an option in average-risk adults older than 50 years, with evolving coverage</cite>.
- Sensitivity to technique and imaging modality: <cite id="7786e884-1">Guidelines standardize air-contrast protocols, contrast-enhanced multiplanar reformations, and dedicated coloncentric analysis to maximize detection</cite>. For right-sided and flat lesions, visualization can still be inferior to direct endoscopic capture. <cite id="7786e884-5">CTC is effective in secondary roles (failed intubation, obstruction) but carries inherent limitations relative to direct endoscopy</cite>.

## Comparative context: vs fecal occult blood test (FOBT) and vs colonoscopy

- FOBT remains proven to reduce CRC mortality and is broadly recommended in many guidelines as a noninvasive annual option. <cite id="bc6adcc9-0">Randomized clinical trials demonstrate FOBT reduces CRC mortality; European and other programs widely adopt FOBT as first-line screening</cite>.
- In the same general population screening context, colonoscopy and CTC yield similar detection of advanced lesions, with colonoscopy offering the advantage of immediate polypectomy. <cite id="98ad0bb2-6">CTC and colonoscopy resulted in similar detection rates for advanced neoplasias within the same general population, establishing CTC as an effective alternative</cite>.
- Direct accuracy trade-offs for CRC screening:
  - CTC can achieve high sensitivity for cancers and ≥10 mm polyps but lags for small and flat/nonpolypoid lesions and sessile serrated polyps. <cite id="bc6adcc9-5">CTC sensitivity for colorectal cancer is about 96.1%, specificity 79.6%–93.1%</cite> <cite id="0abf705b-4">CTC sensitivity falls to 75%–80% for nonpolypoid adenomas</cite> <cite id="0abf705b-0">Colonoscopy more often detects high-risk sessile serrated polyps than CTC</cite>.
  - Colonoscopy detects most lesions (including small sessile polyps) and enables immediate therapeutic intervention, with very high detection of ≥10 mm lesions. <cite id="0abf705b-6">Colonoscopy detects 98% of 10-mm or larger lesions vs 59% for CTC in head-to-head comparisons</cite>.

## Practical recommendations and use-cases

- Average-risk adults: CT colonography can be considered as a screening option every 1–2 years, especially for those averse to sedation or unable to undergo endoscopy, with counseling on radiation and possible extracolonic findings. <cite id="98ad0bb2-5">Guidance emphasizes the ionizing radiation and uncertain benefit from extracolonic findings for screening CTC</cite> <cite id="7786e884-4">Practice parameters define indications for diagnostic CTC, including surveillance after colonic neoplasm</cite> <cite id="7786e884-2">CTC is indicated for screening individuals at average or moderate risk and for surveillance of patients with a history of neoplasm</cite>.
- When colonoscopy fails or is contraindicated: CTC provides a safe, effective alternative pathway to detect neoplasia and change management, including preoperative staging. <cite id="7786e884-5">CTC appears effective and safe when an obstructing CRC prevents complete endoscopic assessment or cecal intubation fails</cite>.
- Patient counseling: highlight no-sedation and short visit, but also the bowel prep burden, risk of extracolonic findings prompting extra workup, and lower yields for small/flat lesions compared with colonoscopy. <cite id="7786e884-9">Radiation exposure is a key limitation; guidelines caution that extracolonic findings may necessitate follow-up tests</cite> <cite id="7786e884-0">CTC requires full bowel prep but saves time and avoids sedation</cite>.

## Bottom line

CT-based colon imaging delivers a noninvasive, outpatient screening option with performance similar to colonoscopy for finding advanced neoplasia and excellent sensitivity for larger polyps and cancers. Its principal limitations are ionizing radiation, dependence on bowel preparation quality and technique, higher miss rates for small, flat, and sessile-serrated lesions compared with colonoscopy, potential over-investigation from extracolonic findings, and variable access and cost; however, policy changes are expanding coverage for screening CTC. <cite id="98ad0bb2-6">CTC and colonoscopy show similar advanced neoplasia detection in screening trials</cite> <cite id="bc6adcc9-5">CTC cancer sensitivity around 96% for large lesions and specificity 79.6%–93.1%</cite> <cite id="98ad0bb2-2">Lower perforation risk than colonoscopy</cite> <cite id="7786e884-7">Medicare coverage for screening CTC became standard effective Jan 1, 2025</cite> <cite id="98ad0bb2-5">Radiation and uncertain downstream harms from extracolonic findings remain key limitations</cite> <cite id="0abf705b-0">Colonoscopy outperforms CTC for high-risk sessile serrated polyps</cite> <cite id="7786e884-5">CTC is a valued rescue test when endoscopy is incomplete</cite>.

original_query: What clinical methods and observations are recommended for assessing tongue function and mobility in infants suspected of having ankyloglossia?
query_without_term: What clinical methods and observations are recommended for assessing tongue function and mobility in infants suspected of having tongue-tie?
answer_original_query:
Below is an evidence‑based approach to assessing tongue function and mobility in infants suspected of having ankyloglossia. The recommendations integrate history, feeding observations, bedside oral motor exams, standardized tools, and objective feeding measures, and they emphasize multidisciplinary evaluation before deciding on intervention.

Summary of the recommended assessment approach
- Start with a detailed history of feeding (latch, transfer, pain, duration, growth, nipple/breast damage) and caregiver concerns, then perform a thorough oral cavity exam evaluating tongue movement in calm and feeding states; treat ankyloglossia only when feeding dysfunction is documented and persists despite skill‑based support and early intervention strategies.<cite id="3b811967-8">A detailed clinical breastfeeding assessment, before the decision to treat a tongue-tie, should include the maternal history taking and physical examination of infant structure and function</cite><cite id="3b811967-0">During the clinical examination of an infant's oral cavity, it is important to assess the tongue's movement and function in a calm position</cite><cite id="3b811967-3">Ankyloglossia is a condition present at birth that restricts the tongue's range of motion because of a short or tight band of tissue called the lingual frenulum</cite><cite id="3b811967-8">A detailed clinical breastfeeding assessment, before the decision to treat a tongue-tie, should include the maternal history taking and physical</cite><cite id="3b879084-8">A clinical assessment of feeding, including the infant swallow, the infant tongue sweep from side to side, and milk flow between swallowing cycles, is essential</cite>.
- Use a standardized bedside mobility tool (e.g., Hazelbaker Assessment Tool for Lingual Frenulum Function/ATLFF) to quantify mobility and guide risk‑stratified referral or treatment planning, alongside direct observation of task‑relevant movement during calm and feeding contexts.<cite id="045805bb-0">The Hazelbaker Assessment Tool for Lingual Frenulum Function (HATLFF) has been developed to give a quantitative assessment of the tongue-tie and recommendation</cite><cite id="3b811967-2">A systematic review evaluated the prevalence of ankyloglossia and assessed tools to assist with tongue-tie identification, highlighting Hazelbaker measurement of tongue lateralization and protrusion</cite><cite id="3b811967-6">Hazelbaker scores consistent with significant ankyloglossia have been shown to be highly correlated with difficulty with latching the infant onto the breast</cite><cite id="045805bb-3">The Hazelbaker Assessment Tool for Lingual Frenulum Function (HATLFF) demonstrates high inter-rater reliability for frenotomy recommendations</cite>.

Parent/caregiver history and feeding observations
- Elicit details on latch quality, infant stay‑attached time, milk transfer, frequency of slips/coming off, maternal nipple or breast pain/damage, and growth; these observations are the main drivers for further functional assessment.<cite id="5c37a82a-1">Evaluation should combine maternal history and infant feeding assessment, including pain, latch, milk transfer, and growth</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-2">Ankyloglossia is defined as a restrictive lingual frenulum that causes problems with breastfeeding that are not improved with lactation support</cite><cite id="3b811967-1">In breastfeeding, proper movement of the tongue around the nipple is hindered, causing difficulty for the infant to obtain a proper latch</cite><cite id="1007c23d-0">Difficulty breastfeeding due to poor latch, inefficient milk extraction, and maternal nipple pain are common symptoms attributed to ankyloglossia</cite>.
- Track objective signs over several feeds: asymmetric latch, repeated nipple/breast flattening or damage despite corrective positioning, persistent maternal pain despite education, slow transfer, and early cessation; these patterns justify a mobility assessment and possible multidisciplinary support (lactation, ENT/oromaxillofacial surgeon, speech‑language pathologist).<cite id="3b811967-8">A detailed clinical breastfeeding assessment should precede decisions to treat, including maternal history and infant oral function evaluation</cite><cite id="3b811967-6">Higher Hazelbaker scores correlate with latching difficulty, guiding consideration of release</cite><cite id="1007c23d-2">A detailed clinical breastfeeding assessment, before treatment, should include maternal history and physical</cite><cite id="1007c23d-3">When an infant has adequate latch on the nipple, milk flow occurs because the anterior tongue lowers and creates an intraoral vacuum</cite>.

Bedside oral function and mobility assessment
- Oral exam at rest: assess tongue posture, range of motion, and movement quality; look for restriction in protrusion, elevation (depression), and lateralization (and side‑to‑side sweep). Document the frenulum’s length, thickness, and attachment point and how these correlate with movement deficits.<cite id="3b811967-0">Clinicians should assess tongue movement and function in a calm position as part of oral cavity examination</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-4">Evaluation focuses on how the tongue elevates, protrudes, and moves side to side, as well as frenulum appearance, including length, thickness, and attachment</cite><cite id="3b87a82a-4">Examination should include assessment of tongue appearance, shape, position and function both in relaxation and during feeding</cite>.
- Task‑relevant feeding movement while calm: observe the infant’s ability to:
  - Elevate and depress the tongue to create lip seal and suction during latch, enabling milk flow; impaired elevation/depression can cause slipping or inability to maintain a vacuum.<cite id="3b87a82a-4">Examination should include assessment of tongue function in relaxation and during feeding</cite><cite id="1007c23d-3">Adequate latch allows milk flow because the anterior tongue lowers and creates an intraoral vacuum</cite>.
  - Lateralize the tip and sweep laterally to stabilize and compress tissue around the nipple/breast for efficient transfer; persistent inability to lateralize or limited sweep compromises extraction.<cite id="3b811967-0">Assess the tongue's movement and function in a calm position</cite>5c37a82a-8">Clinical assessment should assess infant oral function</cite>5c37a82a-4">Feeding function depends on tongue elevation, protrusion, and side-to-side movement</cite>.
- Practical task list clinicians can use:
  - Protrusion: can the tip extend fully, and does the lip form a seal around it during latch?
  - Lateralization: can the tip move laterally around the nipple or breast to maintain attachment?
  - Depression/elevation: can the anterior tongue lower and depress to create and maintain a vacuum, and elevate for swallow clearance?
  - Side‑to‑side sweep: can the infant perform effective lateral sweeps to distribute vacuum across the areola?
  - Symmetry: latched position and movement symmetry on both sides; asymmetry suggests restricted mobility or compensatory patterns.<cite id="3b811967-0">Assess tongue movement and function in a calm position</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-4">Evaluation focuses on how the tongue elevates, protrudes, and moves side to side</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-8">Clinical assessment should assess infant oral function for feeding issues</cite>.

Use of standardized assessment tools and adjuncts
- Hazelbaker Assessment Tool for Lingual Frenulum Function (ATLFF/HATLFF): apply during calm and feeding states to rate mobility (e.g., protrusion, lateralization, depression, lip‑tie appearance) and use the summary score to stratify risk. The tool is the only widely validated infant tongue‑tie screening/assessment in infants under six months and correlates with functional difficulty such as latching; it also underpins treatment recommendations and postoperative de‑scoring.<cite id="3b811967-2">Systematic review highlights Hazelbaker measurement of infant tongue lateralization and protrusion as key to tongue‑tie identification</cite><cite id="3b811967-6">Hazelbaker scores consistent with significant ankyloglossia correlate with difficulty latching onto the breast</cite><cite id="045805bb-3">High inter‑rater reliability of the Hazelbaker tool supports consistent frenotomy recommendations</cite><cite id="045805bb-0">The Hazelbaker Assessment Tool gives a quantitative assessment and recommendation for infants with tongue‑tie</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-7">The ATLFF remains the only valid and reliable tongue‑tie screening and assessment tool for infants under six months of age regardless of feeding method</cite>.
- Ultrasound (adjunct): point‑of‑care ultrasound to visualize lip/nipple engagement and anterior tongue movement/vacuum formation during latch can help confirm functional deficits and monitor change, with reproducible improvements in nipple position and tongue movement reported after frenotomy; however, it should supplement rather than replace direct clinical observation and parent reporting.<cite id="3b811967-5">A preliminary ultrasound study detected a change in nipple position and tongue movement during a feed after intervention</cite><cite id="045805bb-4">The Function Score can be assessed using only certain movements, simplifying bedside scoring</cite>.

Objective feeding measurements in clinic
- Directly observe and rate latch symmetry, stability, and infant swallow mechanics; document milk transfer (amount/time), maternal pain intensity and damage (e.g., flattening, cracking, bruising), and frequency of refusals; trends across multiple feeds inform functional significance of observed mobility deficits.<cite id="3b879084-8">A clinical assessment of feeding should include the infant swallow, the infant tongue sweep from side to side, and milk flow between swallowing cycles</cite><cite id="1007c23d-1">Frenotomy has been shown to decrease maternal nipple pain, improve latch, and to improve milk transfer</cite><cite id="1007c23d-9">Release is associated with improved maternal nipple pain and improved milk transfer rates</cite>.
- Use simple tools to quantify transfer: weighed containers or syringe‑filled bottles with start and stop times for initial feedings; track rate (mL/min) over baseline to demonstrate functional change when appropriate interventions are applied.<cite id="1007c23d-9">Release improves milk transfer rates</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-1">Care pathways emphasize milk transfer and latch as key clinical outcomes</cite>.

Team‑based evaluation and referral
- Build a multidisciplinary team (pediatric ENT, lactation consultant, oromaxillofacial surgeon, and speech‑language pathologist with newborn swallow expertise) early if feeding dysfunction persists despite skilled latch/pain management and oral motor support; shared decision‑making should weigh functional limitation, caregiver stress, and natural history against risks of overdiagnosis and procedure risks.<cite id="3b811967-8">A detailed clinical breastfeeding assessment, including infant oral function, should precede treatment decisions</cite><cite id="3b811967-9">Infants with concerns about feeding should be reviewed by a trained healthcare professional; history‑taking and clinical examination are essential</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-2">Ankyloglossia is defined by restrictive lingual frenulum causing feeding problems not improved by lactation support</cite>.
- Structured pathways: bedside screening for tongue mobility (Hazelbaker) plus feeding observation checklist can triage to (1) education and follow‑up, (2) lactation/SLP intervention, or (3) ENT/omofacial surgical referral for frenotomy/lipotomy when functional deficits are confirmed and persistent.<cite id="3b811967-2">Hazelbaker measurement supports identification of infants with significant ankyloglossia</cite><cite id="3b811967-6">High Hazelbaker scores correlate with latching difficulty to guide referrals or treatment</cite><cite id="3b811967-1">Proper tongue movement around the nipple is hindered by ankyloglossia, leading to latch difficulty</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-8">Care pathways include a Part 1 Infant Feeding Assessment for possible tongue‑tie issues, focusing on milk transfer and latch</cite>.

Decision making, watchful waiting, and escalation
- Apply watchful waiting with frequent re‑assessment when mobility appears only mildly restricted, feeding is symmetric and adequate for growth, and maternal symptoms improve with positioning/nipple support; reassess at 1–2 weeks and again if persistent or worsening deficits emerge.<cite id="3b811967-3">Ankyloglossia restricts the tongue's range of motion at birth and causes feeding dysfunction when significant</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-4">Restricted mobility affects feeding; evaluation should capture tongue elevation, protrusion, and side‑to‑side movement</cite>.
- Escalate if there is persistent poor latch, asymmetric or unstable latch, recurrent maternal nipple/breast pain/damage unresponsive to lactation care, slow milk transfer, frequent early cessation, poor weight gain, or documented abnormal swallow mechanics suggestive of limited depression/lateralization despite adequate compensatory positioning.<cite id="1007c23d-0">Poor latch, inefficient extraction, and maternal nipple pain are common feeding barriers in ankyloglossia</cite><cite id="1007c23d-3">Milk flow requires anterior tongue depression to create an intraoral vacuum at latch</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-8">Clinical assessment should include swallow and side‑to‑side movement and milk flow between swallowing cycles</cite>.
- If a restrictive frenulum is confirmed and functionally limiting, share risks/benefits of release; postoperatively, re‑assess mobility on the same day/within days and monitor for recurrence; adjunct ultrasound can help confirm improved lip/nipple engagement on follow‑up visits.<cite id="045805bb-3">Hazelbaker scores and recommendations show high inter‑rater reliability, supporting consistent follow‑up decisions for frenotomy</cite><cite id="3b811967-5">Ultrasound showed post‑intervention changes in nipple position and tongue movement during feeds</cite>.

Cautions and limitations
- Avoid overdiagnosis from appearance alone; correlate anatomical findings with functional deficits. AAP/ENT guidance emphasizes that ankyloglossia should be diagnosed when feeding problems persist after lactation support; otherwise, routine observation is appropriate.<cite id="5c37a82a-2">Ankyloglossia is a restrictive frenulum that causes feeding problems not improved with lactation support</cite><cite id="3b811967-3">Ankyloglossia restricts tongue motion from birth, but functional impairment is the diagnostic criterion</cite>.
- Recognize natural variability in frenulum morphology and tongue mobility in asymptomatic infants; use standardized tools validated in infants under six months and repeated serially to avoid premature decisions. Hazelbaker and related tools are the only validated infant‑specific instruments; they reliably differentiate high‑risk patterns and can de‑score after intervention.<cite id="045805bb-0">The Hazelbaker Assessment Tool provides a quantitative assessment</cite><cite id="3b811967-7">A systematic review catalogues assessments of tongue structure and function used to diagnose ankyloglossia in infants 0–12 months</cite><cite id="045805bb-3">High inter‑rater reliability supports consistent clinical use across settings</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical infant assessment flow
1) History and screening: eliciting latch/transfer/pain/damage/growth; initial bedside observation; apply a validated screening tool (Hazelbaker) in calm and feeding states to quantify mobility deficits and correlate with feeding dysfunction.<cite id="3b811967-8">A detailed clinical breastfeeding assessment should include maternal history and infant oral function before treatment</cite><cite id="3b811967-6">Higher Hazelbaker scores predict latching difficulty</cite><cite id="3b87a82a-8">A clinical assessment of feeding should include infant swallow, side‑to‑side sweep, milk flow between cycles</cite>.
2) Bedside oral motor exam: rate protrusion, lateralization, depression/elevation, and lateral sweep; note frenulum features; discuss with caregiver how these movements relate to latch/fill/empty/swallow patterns observed at feeds.<cite id="3b811967-0">Clinicians should assess tongue movement and function in a calm position</cite><cite id="5c37a82a-4">Evaluate elevation, protrusion, and side‑to‑side movement as well as frenulum anatomy</cite>.
3) Objective feeding metrics: time‑milk transfer, pain/damage grading, symmetry and stability of latch; document with video when possible and re‑test after lactation/orthodontic intervention; consider brief ultrasound to visualize lip/nipple engagement and anterior tongue movement.<cite id="5c37a82a-8">Care pathways include assessment of milk transfer and latch as possible tongue‑tie issues</cite><cite id="1007c23d-1">Frenotomy decreased maternal nipple pain, improved latch, and improved milk transfer</cite><cite id="3b811967-5">Ultrasound detected changes in nipple position and tongue movement after intervention</cite>.
4) Team‑based re‑assessment at 7–14 days: confirm change in mobility, reduction in pain/damage, improved transfer; provide anticipatory guidance and prevention of recurrence; consider early surgical input if function remains abnormal despite 2–3 weeks of targeted intervention.<cite id="3b811967-8">A detailed assessment should precede treatment; serial reassessments are appropriate</cite><cite id="3b811967-9">Infants with concerns should be reviewed by a trained professional, with history and clinical examination</cite>.
5) Watchful waiting and parent enablement: in mild cases with acceptable growth and minimal maternal symptoms, provide caregiver‑centered education, positioning, nipple choice, and oral motor stimulation guidance; schedule 1–2 week re‑checks and escalate if red flags emerge.<cite id="3b811967-8">Comprehensive assessment before treatment includes oral function evaluation and counseling</cite><cite id="3b87a82a-4">Examination should include function in relaxation and feeding to guide conservative management</cite>.

By integrating these methods—history and feeding observations, standardized bedside mobility assessment, objective clinic measurements, ultrasound adjuncts, and multidisciplinary coordination—clinicians can reliably identify infants with tongue mobility limitations that are functionally impairing and avoid overdiagnosis or premature intervention. <cite id="5c37a82a-2">Ankyloglossia should be defined by feeding dysfunction unresponsive to lactation support rather than appearance alone</cite><cite id="3b811967-8">Detailed breastfeeding assessment and infant oral function exam should precede treatment decisions</cite><cite id="3b811967-6">Hazelbaker scores that reflect significant ankyloglossia correlate with latching difficulty</cite>.

2) Content‑specific challenges in teaching catchment hydrology
- Process coupling and nonlinearity: Runoff is generated through coupled infiltration, storage, and routing processes that can switch among different regimes (e.g., from Hortonian to saturation excess), producing nonlinear peaks, which are hard to conceptually model for novices. <cite id="0c2b2704-7">This paper aims to identify the degree of non‐linearity of the relationship between event peak runoff and potential controls for different runoff generation</cite>. - Promoting inquiry, student agency, and authentic data: A PCK‑formed teacher designs student‑led investigations with authentic hydrologic data and tools (hydrographs, LiDAR, aerial imagery), aligns roles so students “do hydrology” within their capacity, and integrates ethics and logistics of fieldwork. <cite id="e96f3664-2">Hydrology education should move towards student-led learning formats and simultaneously incorporate recent hydrologic</cite> <cite id="39bc5602-8">curated teaching materials, workshops, and thematic collections</cite>.

4) Illustrative curriculum linkages and assessment
- Micro‑to‑macro modeling: Start with rainfall–runoff trays and soil textural analysis; have students build simple tank/loss‑rate representations, then scale to daily catchment simulators, comparing model discharge sequences to gauged records and iterating explanations. <cite id="f993bd0f-5">Shulman described PCK as “the amalgam of content and pedogy”</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-1">a hands-on modeling tool is developed for students to learn the fundamentals of</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-4">simulates catchment discharge, usually on a daily time step, based on time series of</cite>.

- Uncertainty and nonstationarity framing: After students build and test deterministic models, introduce variability by comparing many small events, then discuss how climate‑change‑related nonstationarity can shift expected runoff regimes—reinforcing probabilistic interpretations and the limits of extrapolation. <cite id="0c2b2704-2">Small events ( may be rainfall or runoff) usually remains high in number during any rainy season on any natural catchment</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-3">understanding the impacts of hydrological non-stationarity on runoff projections</cite>.

- Assessment moves: Use elicited explanations of model mismatch (e.g., daily simulator vs. observed flow) and rubrics that score conceptualization quality, evidence use, and coherence of mechanism changes across scales—core to PCK’s knowledge of curriculum integration and formative assessment. <cite id="f993bd0f-4">Pedagogical content knowledge is a form of knowledge that makes science teachers teachers rather than scientists</cite>.

- Concept and scope. Within catchment hydrology—multi-scaled, nonlinear, and human-connected—teachers’ PCK becomes a bridge between deep hydroscience and accessible learning experiences <cite id="3f56bc3a-0">PCK names that idiosyncratic sense of what is appropriate to teach, at what point, and through what method</cite>.

How PCK Aligns With Content-Specific Challenges in Catchment Hydrology
Catchment hydrology poses several content-specific hurdles that PCK is designed to confront:
- Complexity, coupling, and multi-scale dynamics. Students struggle to integrate rainfall–runoff relationships with subsurface flow, groundwater exchange, and watershed-scale processes; abstract coupling is hard without strong representational support and carefully sequenced tasks <cite id="3f56bc3a-0">PCK underpins pedagogical decision-making for complex hydrologic topics in catchments</cite>. Teachers with strong PCK select and adapt models and analogies to make these couplings visible and tractable to learners <cite id="03a3113a-2">Understanding how topics are organized and presented for diverse learners</cite> <cite id="03a3113a-6">Attending to prior knowledge and strategies when reorganizing complex content</cite>.

- Nonlinear behavior, lags, and emergent outcomes. Linear thinking and naïve causal intuitions often mislead interpretations of rain–runoff timing and storage controls; teachers need diagnostic and intervention tools to address these misconceptions <cite id="ab9c1131-8">Instructional analogies (e.g., leaves to watersheds) are used to scaffold understanding of hydrologic principles and address conceptual barriers</cite>. PCK helps integrate hands-on and computational models that reveal nonlinearity and delay via observable outputs before moving to theory.

- Modeling and data literacy. Moving from equations to process-based modeling is difficult; students often favor mechanistic detail over functional representation and struggle with calibration/validation. PCK guides choosing conceptual models first, then mapping model parameters and outputs back to hydrographs, soil moisture, and groundwater contributions <cite id="ab9c1131-0">Hands-on modeling tools are developed to help students learn fundamentals of hydrologic processes, aligning PCK’s amalgam of content and pedagogy</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-9">Conceptual models are preferred for simplicity and understanding even with predictive limits—useful scaffolds for learners</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-2">A hands-on modeling tool is developed to help students learn the fundamentals of hydrologic processes through practical engagement</cite>.

- Human–environment links and local relevance. Watershed issues (e.g., pollution, flow regulation, climate impacts) demand connecting biophysical processes to societal decisions; teachers need curricula and data that situate models and experiments in students’ own watersheds <cite id="3f56bc3a-2">Watershed place-based learning is proposed to deepen understanding of water quality challenges and connect to place</cite> <cite id="3f56bc3a-3">A “waterscapes” paradigm frames human–environment connections to align pedagogical content and context</cite>.

How PCK Translates to Practice: Strategies That Address These Challenges
- Choose representational routes suited to learner sense-making and adapt them (diagrams, analogs, data visualizations). Teachers with strong PCK “repackage” runoff generation, groundwater connectivity, and watershed responses through layered representations (spatial maps, cross-sections, rating curves) and analogies (leaves to leaf litter routing → overland/stor-age → channel; scale-up to watersheds) <cite id="03a3113a-5">PCK concerns ways of representing and formulating the subject that make it comprehensible</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-8">The leaf/watershed analogy and associated instruction aim to increase students’ understanding of hydrologic principles</cite>.

- Use student-centered, inquiry-rich tasks that foreground process coupling with data. Moving beyond lecture, PCK-guided design favors modeling activities with real hydrographs and local data, where students run “what-if” scenarios to witness lag and baseflow contributions and then connect outputs to antecedent moisture, soil, and land use <cite id="3f56bc3a-1">Hydrology education is evolving from lecture-centered to more student-centered approaches in catchment topics</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-4">There is a consensus that hydrology education should move towards student-led formats and incorporate recent hydrologic insights simultaneously</cite>. Conceptual model building and simple simulations before heavy math help learners grasp hydrologic behavior (linearity vs. nonlinearity, time scales) and calibrate intuitions <cite id="ab9c1131-0">Hands-on conceptual hydrologic modeling tools help students learn fundamentals</cite>.

- Anchor to the local watershed with place-based/engaged projects to motivate relevance and integration. PCK emphasizes curricular connections to learners’ environments: students sample a local stream, build a watershed profile, compare rainfall–runoff water balances, and propose monitoring or management plans. This bridges process knowledge to water quality and policy problems <cite id="3f56bc3a-2">Place-based watershed learning targets K–12 engagement with fresh water challenges</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-6">Model My Watershed connects school science to the students’ local watershed, linking content with real-world place</cite>.

- Integrate community resources, modules, and professional learning to sustain expertise. PCK depends on access to high-quality resources and collaborative learning design; communities like HydroLearn share vetted modules and pedagogical strategies across institutions, while professional development supports building and refining PCK for watershed topics <cite id="3f56bc3a-9">A learner-centered approach to watershed hydrology calls for more teach-yourself and learner-controlled resources</cite> <cite id="3f56bc3a-7">Grand Challenges for Hydrology Education call for building international education communities and shared learning networks to support teacher capacity</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-9">Use of community resources and collaborative design helps align PCK components over time</cite>.

Evidence Cycles: From PCK to Improved Learning in Watershed Topics
- The HESS synthesis notes that PCK-oriented decisions (what/when/how) are central for making catchment hydrology teachable, urging a shift beyond teacher-centered delivery to methods that reflect the content’s complexity; it explicitly positions PCK as the organizing lens for curricularizing hydroscience <cite id="3f56bc3a-0">PCK is the organizing principle for what and how to teach in catchments</cite> <cite id="3f56bc3a-1">A review and synthesis advocate more student-centered approaches in catchment hydrology</cite>. 

- Complementary work shows that hands-on modeling tools and local watershed projects align PCK mechanisms—content modeling, learner-centered delivery, and place-based relevance—to strengthen conceptual understanding before adding complexity and data analysis demands <cite id="ab9c1131-0">A hands-on modeling tool helps students learn fundamentals</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-6">Project-based local watershed modeling connects content to real contexts</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-8">Analogy-supported instruction scaffolds hydrologic principles</cite>.

Practical Mapping: PCK Components to Classroom Moves in Catchment Hydrology
- Content knowledge → select core, transferable processes: rainfall–runoff mechanisms, infiltration/throughfall/exfiltration, storage and lag, groundwater–stream exchange, watershed connectivity, and scale effects; connect to climate and human impacts <cite id="03a3113a-3">Content knowledge forms the foundation of PCK</cite> <cite id="03a3113a-5">Formulating the subject in comprehensible ways</cite>.

- Pedagogical content knowledge → repurpose representations and tasks: layered diagrams (energy/ water fluxes), topographic/water-table cross-sections, rating curves; rainfall–runoff “lab-in-the-field” tasks; conceptual model building then testing with simple digital tools; emphasize emergent properties and nonlinearity <cite id="03a3113a-2">Organizing, presenting, adapting topics to learners’ diverse needs</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-9">Use conceptual models for simplicity and insight despite predictive limits</cite>.

- Knowledge of learners and context → diagnose prior models (e.g., naïve “all rain becomes runoff immediately”), plan sequencing to confront and revise them; design learner-controlled activities with visible outcomes and iterative improvement cycles; integrate community and place through local watersheds and citizen-science data <cite id="03a3113a-6">PCK includes deep knowledge of students’ abilities, strategies, development, attitudes, and prior knowledge</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-6">Local watershed projects connect content and place</cite>.

- Curricular integration → combine core concepts with data analysis, uncertainty, and management decision-making; align assessments to process models, not just equations; leverage shared modules (e.g., HydroLearn) to scaffold PCK growth and sustain communities of practice <cite id="03a3113a-3">Curricular knowledge integrates content and pedagogy into coherent sequences</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-9">Community resources and networks support curricularization of watershed topics</cite>.

Summary: PCK as the Interface Between “Watershed Science” and “How Students Learn”
- In catchment hydrology, PCK provides the design logic that couples sophisticated hydrologic content with learners’ cognitive resources and contextual realities. Teachers with strong PCK recognize the discipline’s nonlinear couplings, time scales, and human stakes, and they translate these into sequenced, hands-on, data-rich, place-based tasks and models that build from intuitive analogies to watershed-scale systems thinking <cite id="03a3113a-1">The “fusion” of subject knowledge with pedagogy that PCK describes is the key lever for making difficult topics comprehensible</cite> <cite id="3f56bc3a-0">HESS reframes teaching design using PCK for catchment topics</cite> <cite id="3f56bc3a-2">Place-based watershed learning motivates and deepens understanding</cite>. Building and sharing PCK—through professional learning and community resources—thus lies at the heart of effective hydrology education <cite id="ab9c1131-4">A shift to student-led formats and modern hydrologic content requires coordinated PCK development</cite> <cite id="3f56bc3a-7">Grand Challenges call for communities and networks to support hydrology education</cite> <cite id="ab9c1131-9">Curricular resources and collaborations operationalize PCK and sustain improvement over time</cite>.

original_query: How do current cervical cancer screening guidelines vary based on a woman's age and HIV status, particularly regarding testing intervals and screening methods?

answer_original_query:
Below is a synthesis of how cervical cancer screening guidelines vary by age and HIV status, focusing on testing intervals and screening methods.

Overview
- Many updated guidelines in high-income settings recommend primary high‑risk HPV testing with reflex linkage to colposcopy for positive HPV or cytology‑based triage, and they tailor intervals by age and immune status. <cite id="7c7927fa-5">Individuals aged 30–65 should undergo clinician-collected primary high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) screening every 5 years, using US Food and Drug Administration–cleared tests</cite> while <cite id="7c7927fa-0">women aged 21–29 are recommended to be screened with cytology alone every 3 years</cite> and <cite id="7c7927fa-6">HPV testing with or without Pap co‑testing every 5 years is recommended for ages 30–65</cite>. 
- HIV status often shifts timing and intervals: earlier introduction, more frequent follow-up, and expedited triage/colposcopy are emphasized in people living with HIV (PLHIV). <cite id="2e8e6adc-0">Lifelong screening is recommended among persons with HIV infection</cite> and <cite id="2e8e6adc-9">cervical cytology is recommended at 6‑month intervals when HPV or co‑testing is recommended annually; cytology annually when 3‑year intervals are otherwise used</cite>. <cite id="2e8e6adc-2">For women with HIV under 30, cervical cytology is the primary mode</cite>, and co‑testing strategies used in average-risk women can extend intervals in older PLHIV with normal results. <cite id="7c7927fa-1">Cytology/HPV co‑testing can allow a prolonged cervical cancer screening interval in women with HIV who are older than 29 years and have normal results</cite>. 
- Cross‑nationally, primary HPV every 5 years in ages similar to 30–65 is increasingly endorsed; programs in the 25–64 or 25–69 age bands further smooth transitions. <cite id="652432c9-9">Cervical screening is available to women and people with a cervix aged 25–64 years, with invitations sent by the program</cite> and <cite id="652432c9-3">people with HIV aged 21–29 use cytology as screening modality</cite>.

Age-based differences in women without HIV
- Ages 21–29: cytology every 3 years is recommended; co-testing may be used, and primary HPV every 5 years is also acceptable in many programs. <cite id="7c7927fa-0">The USPSTF recommends screening for cervical cancer every 3 years with cervical cytology alone in women aged 21 to 29 years</cite>. <cite id="7c7927fa-6">For women 30–65, Pap/HPV co‑testing every 5 years is an option</cite>, and <cite id="7c7927fa-5">primary hrHPV every 5 years is recommended for 30–65</cite>. 
- Ages 30–65: many pathways allow HPV co‑testing (every 5 years) or primary HPV (every 5 years); cytology alone every 3 years is also acceptable. <cite id="7c7927fa-6">In women aged 30 to 65 years, the USPSTF recommends Pap test alone every 3 years or HPV testing with or without Pap co‑testing every 5 years</cite> and <cite id="7c7927fa-0">every 5 years with high‑risk HPV testing using hrHPV assays with reflex HPV genotyping</cite>. 
- Age 65 and older: screening can be stopped after adequate prior negative results; surveillance can continue with HPV-based tests if preferred. <cite id="7c7927fa-8">Womens’ Preventive Services updated guidance added “primary hrHPV testing every 5 years (preferred) for women aged 30–65,” and this step helps manage options when continuing surveillance beyond age 65</cite>. <cite id="652432c9-7">Patients can enter long‑term surveillance with HPV‑based testing every 3 years for a minimum of 25 years, even beyond age 65</cite>. 
- Adolescence/young adults: introduce at sexual debut or 13–15, with Pap/HPV testing and consideration of HPV vaccination. <cite id="7c7927fa-2">HPV vaccination for all individuals may be scheduled at 9–12 years, aligning with standard adolescent vaccines</cite>. <cite id="652432c9-4">Screen for high‑risk HPV starting at 21 years of age to 65 years, or within 2 years of sexual activity</cite>.

How HIV status changes intervals and methods
- General principles: screen for life, manage risk tiers, emphasize cytology/VIA triage, and urgent linkage to colposcopy for positive results or immunosuppression. <cite id="2e8e6adc-0">CDC notes that with HIV, screening interval can be increased to every 3 years when tests are normal and emphasizes lifelong screening among persons with HIV infection</cite> and <cite id="2e8e6adc-9">recommends 6‑month cytology when HPV or co‑testing is recommended annually, with annual cytology if 3‑year intervals are used elsewhere</cite>. 
- By immune status and age:
  - Immunocompetent women with HIV (ages ~21–29): cytology is the primary screening method, with repeat cytology intervals and careful triage. <cite id="2e8e6adc-2">Cervical cytology is the primary mode for cervical cancer screening for women with HIV under 30 years of age</cite>. 
  - Women with HIV (≥30): co-testing can extend intervals in older PLHIV with normal results, but pregnancy and increased HPV prevalence must be considered. <cite id="7c7927fa-1">Co‑testing can allow a prolonged interval in women with HIV older than 29 with normal results</cite> and <cite id="2e8e6adc-3">after negative cytology alone, suggested intervals are 3 years for HIV‑uninfected women vs 1 year for women living with HIV, with shorter intervals driven by higher HPV prevalence and risk</cite>. 
  - Immunocompromised or with advanced HIV/oncologic immunosuppression: much shorter intervals, urgent cytology referral, and careful management of HPV persistence. <cite id="2e8e6adc-9">Cytology at 6‑month intervals when HPV or co‑testing is recommended annually reflects tighter surveillance in high‑risk groups</cite>. <cite id="2e8e6adc-5">Transplantation and end‑stage renal disease guidelines recommend Pap or co‑testing every 6 months for the first year post‑transplant, reflecting heightened risk</cite>. 
  - Pregnancy in PLHIV: prefer cytology-based screening, avoid HPV primary testing during pregnancy if discordant management is unavailable; treat high-grade lesions to reduce mother‑to‑child transmission risk. <cite id="2e8e6adc-2">Women with HIV under 30 use cytology as the primary screen</cite> and <cite id="7c7927fa-1">co‑testing strategies emphasize urgent linkage pathways for abnormalities</cite>. 
- Primary HPV testing in PLHIV: increasingly used with triage to colposcopy; WHO guidance emphasizes primary HPV DNA testing with short intervals in women living with HIV to maximize detection. <cite id="652432c9-2">WHO suggests starting regular cervical cancer screening at age 25 among women living with HIV</cite> and <cite id="652432c9-5">recommends a shorter screening interval of every 3 to 5 years with primary HPV DNA testing for women living with HIV</cite>. 
- Additional HIV‑specific elements: offer screening for cervical and anogenital cancers starting early, and manage sexual‑risk changes (new partners). <cite id="652432c9-0">Screening for cervical and anogenital tract cancer is appropriate for all adult patients, with a dedicated guideline for adults with HIV</cite> and <cite id="652432c9-4">screen women living with HIV from 21 years to 65 years, or within 2 years of sexual activity</cite>. <cite id="7c7927fa-3">HIV-related risk requires individualized, more intensive surveillance, with cytology or co‑testing at shorter intervals when immunosuppressed</cite>.

Screening methods: how they differ by age and HIV status
- Cytology alone (Pap) vs co‑testing vs primary HPV:
  - Average-risk women 21–29: cytology every 3 years. <cite id="7c7927fa-0">Cytology every 3 years is recommended 21–29</cite>. 
  - Average-risk women 30–65: HPV co‑testing every 5 years or primary HPV every 5 years; cytology every 3 years also acceptable. <cite id="7c7927fa-6">HPV testing with or without Pap co‑testing every 5 years</cite> and <cite id="7c7927fa-5">primary hrHPV every 5 years is recommended</cite>. 
  - PLHIV (immunocompetent): cytology is primary modality under 30; co‑testing may lengthen intervals when normal. <cite id="2e8e6adc-2">Cytology is primary for women with HIV under 30</cite>, and <cite id="7c7927fa-1">co‑testing can extend intervals in PLHIV over 29 with normal tests</cite>. 
  - PLHIV (immunocompromised/advanced disease or after immunosuppressive therapy): cytology frequently used to monitor for rapid disease progression, often at 6‑monthly intervals with urgent referral for positives. <cite id="2e8e6adc-9">Cytology every 6 months when HPV or co‑testing is recommended annually due to higher risk</cite>; transplant populations often get Pap or co‑testing every 6 months initially. <cite id="2e8e6adc-5">Pap or co‑testing every 6 months for the first year after solid organ transplantation</cite>. 
  - HPV triage and colposcopy linkage:
    - HPV16/18 positivity or high-grade lesions warrant urgent referral and shortened intervals irrespective of HIV status; in PLHIV, monitoring and ART to restore immunity are central. <cite id="7c7927fa-5">Primary hrHPV every 5 years relies on linkage to colposcopy for positive results, emphasizing triage</cite> and <cite id="2e8e6adc-0">CDC highlights lifelong screening and urgent evaluation for abnormalities in persons with HIV</cite>. 
- HIV‑specific considerations in method choice: where primary HPV is not available, cytology/HPV co‑testing remains foundational with shorter permissible intervals for PLHIV, especially in younger adolescents. <cite id="7c7927fa-4">If primary HPV testing is not available, individuals 25–65 should be screened by co‑testing</cite> and <cite id="2e8e6adc-3">after negative cytology, HIV‑uninfected women can wait 3 years vs 1 year for women living with HIV, reflecting higher risk</cite>. 
- WHO and international policy context: primary HPV every 5 years with 3–5 year alternative ranges for HIV, but earlier initiation and shorter intervals for PLHIV. <cite id="652432c9-5">WHO recommends primary HPV DNA testing every 3–5 years for women living with HIV</cite> and <cite id="652432c9-2">suggests starting screening at age 25 among WLHIV</cite>. <cite id="652432c9-4">ICCP-aligned guidance recommends screening for high‑risk HPV among WLHIV from age 21 to 65 or within 2 years of sexual debut</cite>.

Pregnancy and peripartum considerations
- HIV-positive pregnancy: screen with cytology rather than primary HPV if discordant management is unavailable; treat high-grade lesions in pregnancy to reduce transmission risk, and intensify postpartum surveillance due to risk of human papillomavirus coinfection and lesion progression. <cite id="2e8e6adc-2">Cytology is the primary mode in women with HIV under 30, aligning with peripartum strategies where discordant HPV management is not available</cite> and <cite id="2e8e6adc-9">close cytology follow-up when HPV-positive or co‑tested recommendations are in place due to higher risk</cite>. <cite id="652432c9-0">Pregnancy in PLHIV requires attention to cervical screening and treatment pathways</cite>.

Special contexts and transitions
- From age-based to HPV-based convergence: moving off cytology at age ≥30 favors HPV primary testing every 5 years; in women living with HIV, similar HPV-based pathways apply with shorter intervals to women with immunosuppression and with pregnancy, and earlier start to screening. <cite id="7c7927fa-5">Primary hrHPV testing every 5 years for 30–65 is recommended</cite>, and <cite id="652432c9-5">WHO recommends primary HPV DNA testing with shorter intervals for WLHIV</cite>. 
- After abnormal results: regardless of age/HIV status, colposcopy with targeted biopsy and treatment is indicated for ASC‑CIN2/2+ lesions, with intensified follow-up and linkage to care. <cite id="7c7927fa-9">Women living with HIV and CIN2+ should be referred urgently for colposcopy and treatment</cite>. 
- Transition to NICE-style age bands and programmatic triage: automated invitations and colposcopy referral thresholds at high HPV risk help harmonize start ages and HIV risk streaming in 25–64/69 bands. <cite id="652432c9-9">The UK screening program invites 25–64 year olds and triages high‑risk HPV to urgent referral</cite>.

Putting it together
- If HIV‑negative and sexually active by 25, expect cytology every 3 years (ages 21–29), then either co‑testing every 5 years or primary HPV every 5 years (ages 30–65), with surveillance continuing and potentially tapering after adequate negative history; pregnancies are handled cautiously and cytology‑centric if HPV primary is not preferred/available. <cite id="7c7927fa-6">Pap every 3 years 30–65 by co‑testing</cite>, <cite id="7c7927fa-5">or primary hrHPV every 5 years</cite>, <cite id="652432c9-9">and UK programs screen 25–64 with automated triage</cite>. 
- If HIV‑positive and immunocompetent, start screening earlier (often at sexual debut or ≥21), primarily by cytology under 30, then use HPV co‑testing or primary HPV with triage to colposcopy in older ages; maintain tighter intervals after normal co‑tests. <cite id="2e8e6adc-2">Cytology is primary ≤29 for WLHIV</cite>, <cite id="652432c9-4">screen WLHIV from 21 to 65 or within 2 years of sexual activity</cite>, and <cite id="7c7927fa-1">co‑testing can extend intervals in WLHIV ≥30 with normal results</cite>. 
- If HIV‑positive and immunocompromised (advanced HIV or on immunosuppression), screen lifelong with more frequent cytology at 6‑monthly intervals, urgent triage/colposcopy for HPV positivity or ASC‑CIN2+, pregnancy-specific precautions, and early HIV sexual debut screening. <cite id="2e8e6adc-9">Cytology every 6 months when HPV/co‑testing targets annual evaluation in high‑risk</cite>, <cite id="652432c9-5">WHO endorses primary HPV with shorter 3–5 year cycles in WLHIV</cite>, and <cite id="2e8e6adc-5">transplant guidance supports 6‑month Pap/co‑testing initially</cite>. 
- When resources favor primary HPV, HPV-based pipelines at 3–5 year intervals largely replace cytology for average‑risk women ≥30, while HIV programs substitute earlier entry and shorter intervals in those at elevated risk; when primary HPV is not available, cytology/HPV co‑testing remains recommended with adjusted intervals per age/HIV risk. <cite id="7c7927fa-5">Primary HPV every 5 years in 30–65</cite>, <cite id="7c7927fa-4">co‑testing when primary HPV is unavailable in 25–65</cite>, and <cite id="7c7927fa-0">HPV testing can be combined with cytology for 30–65</cite>. <cite id="652432c9-2">WHO: start at 25 for WLHIV</cite> with <cite id="652432c9-5">primary HPV and shorter intervals</cite>.

Overview
In women, cancer screening intervals and methods vary by age for several cancers, and HIV status further modifies recommendations through higher HPV prevalence, immunosuppression-related disease patterns, and the impact of antiretroviral therapy (ART) on HPV acquisition and cervical disease. Below, key cancers are summarized by age and HIV status, focusing on intervals and screening modalities.

Cervical cancer (primary HPV and Pap-based screening)
- At average risk, age-based recommendations:
  - Ages 21–29: cytology (Pap) alone every 3 years; do not screen before 21; no screening with HPV testing as primary in most guidelines for this age band. <cite id="1b5314ff-0">The USPSTF recommends screening for cervical cancer every 3 years with cervical cytology alone in women aged 21 to 29 years.</cite> <cite id="1b5314ff-2">Screening is not recommended before age 21 years among those at average risk; cytology every 3 years is recommended from 21+ in CDC guidance.</cite> <cite id="1b5314ff-1">Individuals aged 21–29 years should be screened every 3 years with cytology alone.</cite>
  - Ages 30–65: options include cytology alone every 3 years; primary HPV testing alone every 5 years; or co-testing (HPV + cytology) every 5 years. <cite id="1b5314ff-0">For women aged 30–65, USPSTF allows cytology alone every 3 years or combined HPV/ cytology every 5 years (and high-risk HPV alone every 5 years) as acceptable options.</cite> <cite id="1b5314ff-3">In women aged 30–65, acceptable strategies include cytology-only every 3 years, high-risk HPV alone every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years.</cite> <cite id="1b5314ff-4">Women aged 30–65 should be screened with primary hrHPV testing every 5 years or with co-testing every 5 years; cytology-only every 3 years is also acceptable.</cite> <cite id="1b5314ff-5">Primary HPV testing is now widely recommended for ages 25–65; co-testing is an alternative if primary HPV is not available, with 5-year intervals.</cite> <cite id="1b5314ff-6">ACS/USPSTF now recommend initiating cervical cancer screening at age 25 with primary HPV screening, with Pap/HPV co-testing also acceptable 25–65.</cite>
- HIV-related modifications (additional risk due to HPV):
  - WHO 2021: start HPV DNA–based cervical screening at age 25 with 3–5-year intervals. <cite id="255c7591-3">WHO recommends HPV DNA detection as part of a screen–triage–treat approach starting at age 25, with regular screening every 3 to 5 years.</cite>
  - For women with HIV, normal co-testing results allow the same age-based interval extension as in non-HIV contexts, provided ART is suppressed; otherwise, closer surveillance is advised. <cite id="255c7591-1">Cytology/HPV co-testing can allow a prolonged cervical cancer screening interval in women with HIV who are older than 29 years and have normal cytology and HPV results.</cite> <cite id="d77df595-0">Co-testing with a prolonged interval is allowed for HIV+ women over 29 with normal results.</cite>
  - Clinical management emphasizes earlier initiation, evaluation of cervical abnormalities with colposcopy, and the benefit of ART (reduces HPV acquisition and regression, lowers progression). <cite id="d77df595-1">ART reduces HPV acquisition, improves regression, and decreases rates of cervical disease progression in women with HIV.</cite> <cite id="d77df595-1">Screening and treatment to prevent cervical cancer are strengthened by ART, which reduces HPV acquisition and progression.</cite>
  - Regional HIV guidelines support age-based cervical screening (25 and above) and cytology- or HPV-based intervals, with annual review if positive tests/abnormalities occur. <cite id="255c7591-3">HIV-associated guidelines emphasize HPV-based screening at 25 with 3–5-year intervals and triage/treatment.</cite> <cite id="255c7591-9">The guideline update for HIV care details co-testing and interval decisions based on HIV-related risk and immune status.</cite> <cite id="d77df595-3">The NYSDOH AI guideline supports age-based cervical cancer screening for any patient with HIV who has or had a cervix.</cite>
  - Immunocompetent adolescents and young women with HIV should still begin age-adjacent screening (Pap/HPV), recognizing higher HPV burden; intervals shorten if ART is not suppressed or prior high-grade lesions exist. <cite id="d77df595-1">In women with HIV, normal co-testing can permit 3–5-year intervals; otherwise, shorter intervals and higher surveillance are warranted in immune dysfunction.</cite> <cite id="d77df595-5">Adults with HIV older than 29 and with normal co-testing can extend intervals per age bands, under HIV guidance frameworks.</cite>
  - For adolescents/13–21: Pap/HPV testing is not recommended before age 21; HPV testing is not primary, whereas cytology (Pap) yields a longer interval with negative results. <cite id="1b5314ff-2">Screening is not recommended before age 21 for average-risk individuals; CDC emphasizes HPV-based screening from 30 onward.</cite> <cite id="1b5314ff-5">In adolescents and young adults under 25, ACS aligns with starting primary HPV at 25, with Pap/HPV co-testing available when appropriate.</cite> <cite id="d77df595-2">Guidelines clarify age-based screening and test selection by decade in adolescents.</cite>
- After a negative HPV result in the screening setting, repeat testing in 3 years is standard in non-HIV average-risk women; for women living with HIV, shorter intervals and closer monitoring are commonly advised if immune suppression persists, but may be extended with sustained ART suppression and negative co-tests; WHO recommends 3–5-yearly repeats starting at 25 with HPV-based programs. <cite id="255c7591-5">Repeat testing after negative self-collected vaginal HPV testing is recommended in 3 years in screening settings.</cite> <cite id="255c7591-2">For HIV-uninfected women, 3-year intervals after negative cytology; for women living with HIV, intervals shorten to 1 year after cytology with HPV positivity, and clinical context matters.</cite> <cite id="255c7591-3">WHO indicates 3–5-yearly screening after initial HPV-based detection with triage and treat.</cite>

Breast cancer screening (age and HIV)
- Average-risk, non-HIV women:
  - Begin at 40–45 or 50, with biennial screening mammography to 74–79; individualized decisions for 76–85 and no screening after 85 per USPSTF. <cite id="1b5314ff-2">USPSTF recommends starting screening mammography at 40–44 with biennial screening until 74–79 and individualized decisions 76–85.</cite> <cite id="00790632-0">USPSTF suggests flexible sigmoidoscopy/FIT and colonoscopy every 10 years from 45–49 for colorectal; analogous age-tailored decisions for breast screening at 40–75+ with biennial to annual patterns.</cite> <cite id="00790632-1">CDC and major guidelines emphasize shared decision-making for breast screening starting at recommended ages, with tailoring by risk and comorbidities, including older adults.</cite>
- HIV status:
  - There are no universal, single-test interval changes for all women with HIV; risk is individualized and often escalated due to immunosuppression and potential earlier onset of breast pathology. Clinical HIV guidelines integrate breast screening into risk-based counseling starting at age-equivalent thresholds (e.g., 40–50) with attention to additional risk factors, and imaging modality choice (mammography, ultrasound, MRI per indication) is tailored to life expectancy and risk. <cite id="00790632-8">Guideline summaries emphasize test selection (mammography, ultrasound, MRI) and age-specific starts (e.g., at or after 50), with individualized approaches for women with HIV-related risk profiles.</cite> <cite id="00790632-9">ACS and other cancer society guidance recommend shared decision-making about breast screening modality and timing for women with complex HIV-related risks, emphasizing life expectancy and comorbidities.</cite> <cite id="00790632-7">Individualized, selective screening from 76 to 85 is explicitly advised in USPSTF-type frameworks, reflecting HIV risk tailoring.</cite>
  - Routine screening mammography intervals should be aligned with the same age thresholds with attention to CD4 count, ART exposure, and the presence of risk factors (e.g., BRCA, family history); if CD4 is very low or prior significant abnormalities, earlier or additional imaging may be prudent. <cite id="00790632-9">Visual and adjunct screening strategies are tailored to older individuals and those with complex histories; clinical guidance for women with HIV emphasizes individualized schedules.</cite>

Colorectal cancer screening (age and HIV)
- Average-risk women:
  - Generally start at 45–50 (USPSTF/ACS), with options: colonoscopy every 10 years; flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5–10 years; fecal immunochemical test (FIT) or stool DNA (gFIT) annually or every 1–3 years. <cite id="00790632-0">USPSTF recommends colonoscopy every 10 years, FIT or sigmoidoscopy with annual or 5-yearly intervals, and individualized decisions beyond 75.</cite> <cite id="00790632-1">CDC summarizes similar test options with shared decision-making for those 76–85 and older asymptomatic individuals.</cite> <cite id="00790632-3">Acceptable colorectal screening options for adults include colonoscopy every 10 years, flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and fecal DNA tests every 1–3 years or FIT annually.</cite> <cite id="00790632-5">USPSTF suggests sigmoidoscopy every 5 years or with FIT annually every 10 years; stool-based tests carry their own cadence.</cite>
- Women living with HIV:

Programs may initiate screening at 25 years or upon sexual debut plus 5 years, with interval adjustments based on immune status and ART. <cite id="255c7591-4">HIV guidelines call for screening for cervical cancer in any person living with HIV with a cervix, with extension of age-based programs.</cite> <cite id="d77df595-1">ART reduces HPV acquisition and disease progression across sites; clinical programs integrate HPV-directed screening/triage logic in HIV.</cite>

  - Routine skin examination is used in some HIV programs beginning at 12–24 weeks after ART initiation and every 3–12 months thereafter while immune reconstitution occurs; persistent or enlarging nodules prompt biopsy. The role of whole-body skin examination beyond focal exams in immunocompetent patients is not standard and is individualized. <cite id="d77df595-8">Guidelines include skin examination strategies around immune restoration in adults/adolescents with HIV, with emphasis on KS and lymphoma.</cite>
