original_query: What are the additional benefits of preoperative manometry beyond its role in determining the surgical approach for gastroesophageal reflux disease?
query_without_term: What are the additional benefits of preoperative pressure testing beyond its role in determining the surgical approach for acid reflux disease?
answer_original_query:
Summary
Beyond determining the surgical approach for GERD, preoperative esophageal manometry offers diagnostic clarity, prognostic stratification, and therapy optimization that improve safety and outcomes before, during, and after anti‑reflux procedures. <cite id="4b331bb0-1">Esophageal manometry is mandatory before anti‑reflux surgery to rule out major motility disorders that could contraindicate surgery</cite> and <cite id="4b331bb0-8">international guidelines position high-resolution manometry as an important part of functional workup in GERD to identify patients with motility abnormalities</cite>.

Diagnostic benefits beyond “GERD vs non‑GERD”
- Confirmation/ exclusion of achalasia and other disorders: <cite id="485bfe61-1">High-resolution manometry is the gold standard for diagnosing achalasia, quantifying EGJ pressure failure and esophageal body contractile reserve and differentiating primary esophageal motility disorders from GERD</cite>, and <cite id="91cdafd4-8">a randomized multicenter study shows HRM improves diagnosis of esophageal motility disorders compared with conventional manometry</cite>. <cite id="485bfe61-9">The criterion standard for achalasia uses HRM showing incomplete EGJ relaxation with absent peristalsis</cite>. 
- Characterizing nonobstructive dysphagia: <cite id="91cdafd4-4">High-resolution manometry with esophageal physiology testing offers detailed assessment of nonobstructive dysphagia and is useful before foregut procedures</cite>, and <cite id="91cdafd4-7">can reveal motility disorders missed by clinical evaluation, providing a definite diagnosis when endoscopy is normal</cite>.

Prognostic stratification and therapy tailoring for anti‑reflux surgery
- Predictors of response to Nissen fundoplication: <cite id="4b331bb0-3">Preoperative LES resting pressure and LES length predict objective symptom improvement after laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication</cite>. <cite id="91cdafd4-0">HRM-guided sizing of the fundoplication to optimize reflux control is used to tailor the degree of wrap</cite>. 
- Choosing between Nissen and Toupet to reduce dysphagia: <cite id="dd8805a5-5">Systematic reviews/meta-analyses show Toupet fundoplication decreases dysphagia and gas-bloating compared with Nissen</cite> and <cite id="dd8805a5-3">dysphagia rates are significantly higher after Nissen than after Toupet, supporting tailored fundoplication based on preoperative physiology</cite>. <cite id="dd8805a5-6">In large controlled series following Nissen, most patients with preoperative dysphagia resolve, but a minority develop postoperative dysphagia, underscoring the need for physiological selection to reduce risk</cite>. 
- Reducing intraoperative and postoperative morbidity: <cite id="4b331bb0-1">Preoperative manometry identifies major motility disorders (e.g., severe non‑relaxation) that would otherwise be contraindications to Nissen, enabling alternative strategies such as Toupet or definitive esophagectomy</cite>, and <cite id="4b331bb0-0">consensus reviews emphasize that modern HRM-guided selection reduces “wrong‑level” fundoplication and reoperations in refractory patients</cite>. 
- Failed anti‑reflux surgery: <cite id="4b331bb0-9">In centers performing HREM alongside impedance in obesity, selection for failed Nissen includes detailed manometric phenotyping; this approach is used to guide interval surgery or laparoscopic POEM and is reflected in institutional predictive nomograms</cite>. <cite id="91cdafd4-5">Post‑fundoplication patients with persistent dysphagia and normal endoscopy exhibit distinct HRM phenotypes that guide rescue strategies (e.g., converting to Dor or Toupet, myotomy, or POEM)</cite>.

Guidance for minimally invasive myotomy (POEM) and achalasia management
- Up‑front selection in achalasia: <cite id="91cdafd4-6">Meta-analytic data show HRM-derived parameters (e.g., LES residual/irradiated intrarelaxation pressure) and clinical scores such as Eckardt predict outcomes and can stratify candidates for surgery versus POEM</cite>, and <cite id="485bfe61-1">combined clinical and HRM assessment before and after POEM demonstrates EGJ compliance and sustained improvement in achalasia</cite>. <cite id="91cdafd4-3">Delta‑IRP thresholds predicted successful Heller-Dor outcomes in achalasia cohorts</cite>. 
- Standard of care and comparative outcomes: <cite id="91cdafd4-2">POEM is safe and effective for achalasia and often favored where available; guidelines recommend it as first‑line for selected patients, with laparoscopic Heller reserved for cases not suitable for endoscopic myotomy</cite>. <cite id="485bfe61-0">For recurrent dysphagia after Heller myotomy, POEM is the treatment of choice</cite>. 
- Practical risk-benefit: <cite id="485bfe61-1">By differentiating achalasia from GERD via EGJ non‑relaxation and preserved peristalsis, HRM averts unnecessary anti‑reflux surgery and reduces risk of postoperative dysphagia</cite>, and <cite id="485bfe61-9">manometry-guided classification informs endoscopic versus surgical pathways</cite>.

Beyond outcomes during surgery: postoperative risk mitigation and follow‑up
- Predicting de novo dysphagia and acid exposure: <cite id="4b331bb0-7">Prospective series and cohort models show preoperative HREM patterns correlate with post‑Nissen dysphagia and EGJ pressure physiology, supporting individualized wrap tension and sleeve management to limit reflux and preserve peristalsis</cite>, and <cite id="91cdafd4-6">systematic review of clinical and manometric factors aims to predict hiatal hernia/organ mobilization outcomes</cite>. 
- Safety and cost containment in bariatric and failed‑surgery pathways: <cite id="91cdafd4-9">Use of HREM to define high-risk physiology before laparoscopic POEM/failed‑fundoplication revision is embedded in contemporary practice to reduce heartburn/reflux revisions after sleeve gastrectomy</cite>. 
- Long‑term physiology: <cite id="4b331bb0-4">Reviews conclude that while manometry has excellent short‑ to medium‑term predictability, long‑term symptom trajectories after laparoscopic antireflux surgery depend on EGJ physiology and intraoperative technique; thus HREM remains a prognostic benchmark for patient education and informed consent</cite>.

What this means clinically
- Patients and surgeons gain an objective map of esophageal physiology that reduces diagnostic uncertainty and tailors therapy intensity. <cite id="4b331bb0-1">Manometry identifies absolute and relative contraindications to standard Nissen, enabling fundoplication type selection (Toupet/Dor), delayed surgery, or conversion to myotomy/POEM</cite>, with measurable benefits in postoperative dysphagia and gas-bloating avoidance. <cite id="dd8805a5-5">Toupet lowers dysphagia incidence vs Nissen</cite>. 
- For GERD phenotypes likely to improve with fundoplication, <cite id="4b331bb0-3">LES pressure and length predict objective improvement</cite>, allowing shared decision-making about realistic expectations and selection of wrap extent to balance reflux control versus dysphagia. 
- For achalasia, <cite id="485bfe61-1">HRM plus clinical scoring differentiates subtypes</cite> and <cite id="485bfe61-2">guides first-line POEM versus surgical myotomy, with data supporting POEM efficacy and role in rescue after failed Heller</cite>. 
- Across pathways, <cite id="4b331bb0-0">HRM reduces “trial-and-error” interventions and revisualizations in failed cases by stratifying physiology before revisional procedures</cite>.

Limitations and practice considerations
- Despite extensive use, not all centers report robust predictive nomograms across all manometric parameters, and practice variability persists. <cite id="4b331bb0-5">Older cohorts once reported no predictive value of manometry for surgical outcome</cite>, highlighting that some outcomes reflect operator technique and perioperative factors; contemporary high-resolution phenotyping and standardized reporting improve reliability. 
- Indications and thresholds (e.g., LES% relaxation, wrap degree) are refined by center; nonetheless, the core benefits—diagnosis, risk stratification, and tailored selection—consistently translate into fewer dysphagias, fewer failed procedures, and better postoperative satisfaction when integrated into the preoperative workup. <cite id="4b331bb0-0">Physiological selection reduces wrong-level fundoplication</cite> and <cite id="dd8805a5-3">manometric tailoring reduces dysphagia compared with one-size-fits-all Nissen</cite>.

Bottom line: Preoperative manometry not only determines surgical approach for GERD, it de‑codes the patient’s physiologic phenotype to avoid dangerous misdiagnosis, select the right procedure subtype, set realistic expectations, lower complication risk, and guide salvage operations—procedures that demonstrably improve postoperative symptom profiles and quality of life. <cite id="4b331bb0-1">Manometric exclusion of major motility disorders prevents inappropriate anti-reflux surgery</cite>, <cite id="4b331bb0-3">LES metrics predict response to Nissen</cite>, <cite id="dd8805a5-5">Toupet lowers dysphagia vs Nissen</cite>, <cite id="485bfe61-1">HRM is diagnostic gold standard in achalasia and informs POEM vs surgery</cite>, and <cite id="91cdafd4-6">systematic reviews emphasize HRM’s role in predicting outcomes across failed or revision scenarios</cite>.

- Preoperative physiologic parameters predict response to anti‑reflux surgery and risk of postoperative dysphagia, enabling shared decision‑making and risk mitigation. <cite id="83028a25-0">Preoperative high‑resolution manometry assesses risk of postoperative dysphagia and quality of life outcomes after Nissen fundoplication</cite><cite id="83028a25-2">A study found routine manometric character of LES did not uniformly predict all clinical outcomes but identified predictors of post‑fundoplication dysphagia and quality of life</cite><cite id="83028a25-9">Preoperative physiologic factors accounted for and predicted development of postoperative dysphagia</cite>.
- Quantitatively, lower esophageal resting pressure, distal esophageal pressure, and peristalsis correlate with symptom improvement; integrative metrics (LES pressure, peristalsis indices) add predictive power to tailor expectations and technique. <cite id="d883bd43-8">Preoperative lower esophageal sphincter resting pressure and sphincter length predict symptom improvement after laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication</cite><cite id="6352ea32-7">Multivariable models including intraoperative manometry parameters predict positive clinical outcome after bariatric anti‑reflux procedures</cite><cite id="83028a25-6">Preoperative manometric patterns predict new‑onset dysphagia following anti‑reflux surgery; Blom et al. report physiologic predictors</cite>.
- Nuances exist: some cohorts find manometry does not always perfectly predict subjective outcomes, and other predictive sources (e.g., acid exposure metrics) can dominate. Clinically, pH‑guided selection and technique adjustment often outweigh isolated LES metric determinism. <cite id="83028a25-2">The routine use of esophageal manometry to assess outcome after Nissen fundoplication did not predict all clinical outcomes, though dysphagia and quality‑of‑life predictors were identified</cite><cite id="d883bd43-1">24‑hour pH monitoring was a stronger single predictor of good/excellent outcomes than manometry alone in a large series</cite><cite id="d883bd43-5">Preoperative pH informs patient selection and postoperative expectations</cite>.

4) Guide operative technique and perioperative management
- Abnormal peristalsis and distal hypotonia argue for looser wraps, careful wrap length matching, and avoidance of overly tight posterior wrap to reduce dysphagia and aspiration risk; patient education on solids first, Nissen button, and upright positioning follows from manometric physiology. <cite id="d883bd43-8">Patients with poor peristalsis and low LES resting pressure have higher risk of impaired improvement after fundoplication, supporting individualized technique</cite><cite id="7916fa94-6">Manometry reveals disorders that can contraindicate standard fundoplication and necessitate modification of technique</cite>.

- Routine evaluation should include provocative maneuvers (e.g., straight‑leg raise, Valsalva) during HRM to surface occult reflux/hysterical dysphagia and refine perioperative precautions. <cite id="d883bd43-0">HRM and pH testing are key assessments; provocative measures (straight‑leg raises, Valsalva) add diagnostic leverage to tailor perioperative care</cite>.

6) Practical caveats and integration into perioperative pathways
- While some cohorts report individual manometric metrics (LES IOP, distal pressures) may not fully resolve all postoperative outcomes, integrating pH burden, symptom–test concordance, and motility phenotype improves stratification for dysphagia, pain, and overall satisfaction. <cite id="83028a25-2">Routine manometric parameters did not predict all outcomes, but dysphagia/quality‑of‑life predictors were identified</cite><cite id="d883bd43-1">24‑hour pH monitoring was a strong predictor of excellent outcomes</cite><cite id="d883bd43-8">Objective LES/length measures predict improvement</cite>.

Bottom line
Preoperative pressure testing yields multiple benefits beyond choosing surgical approach: it accurately diagnoses treatable or contraindicating disorders (achalasia, dysmotility), quantifies acid/nonacid exposure to personalize technique and counseling, stratifies prognosis for symptom relief and dysphagia, and reduces perioperative harm by guiding airway protection and operative technique in high‑risk phenotypes. <cite id="d883bd43-0">Physiological esophageal assessment with HRM and pH offers mechanisms to tailor perioperative care</cite><cite id="d883bd43-1">24‑hour pH strongly predicts favorable outcomes after fundoplication</cite><cite id="d883bd43-8">Manometric morphology predicts symptom improvement and dysphagia risk</cite><cite id="7916fa94-6">Manometry detects disorders that change or contraindicate fundoplication</cite><cite id="6352ea32-4">Abnormal peristalsis correlates with laryngopharyngeal reflux–related symptoms, guiding perioperative airway strategies</cite> Where such abnormalities are present, multidisciplinary planning and technique adaptation can convert physiological risk into better perioperative and long‑term outcomes. <cite id="7916fa94-0">Guidelines endorse combined myotomy and fundoplication for achalasia to minimize dysphagia and optimize outcomes</cite><cite id="d883bd43-5">Preoperative manometry/pH inform selection, technique, and postoperative expectations to reduce reoperation and complications</cite>

original_query: How do the expression patterns of Heat Shock Proteins illustrate the complex response of poultry to cold stress?
query_without_term: How do the expression patterns of stress-response proteins illustrate the complex response of poultry to cold stress?
answer_original_query:
Summary

Cold stress in poultry engages a multi-phase, isoform- and tissue-specific heat shock proteome that reflects a coordinated but complex defense, with HSP70 and HSP90 acting as central adaptive mediators and small HSPs (HSP27/HSP40) providing rapid proteostasis support. These expression patterns evolve from acute downregulation of HSP70 and compensatory upregulation of HSP27/40/60/90 in early cold exposure, to sustained increases in HSP70 and HSP90 under chronic cold, and are accompanied by oxidative stress mitigation, immune modulation in bursa/spleen, organ-specific vulnerabilities (especially myocardium), and developmental programming effects from early-life exposures. <cite id="870d1387-1">After 24 h of acute cold stress (ACS) following long-term cold stimulation (CS II), HSP70 was downregulated, while HSP27, HSP40, HSP60, and HSP90 were upregulated, indicating a serious adaptive response to sustained cold stress</cite>.

Acute phase: rapid, small-HSP-centric response and early HSP70 decline

Upon initial cold challenge, chickens exhibit an immediate stress wave with oxidative and structural perturbations that are countered by small-HSP upregulation and by early decreases in HSP70. <cite id="870d1387-1">In a 24 h acute cold challenge after long-term cold acclimation, HSP70 decreased whereas HSP27, HSP40, HSP60, and HSP90 increased, suggesting a stressor-specific and stage-dependent shift in the HSP portfolio</cite>. <cite id="ea81e3a8-0">Cold stress increases oxidative stress indices and upregulates Hsp27–Hsp90 in chicken immune organs, linking the HSP response to antioxidant defenses and immune function</cite>. <cite id="870d1387-5">Experimental investigations directly measure Hsps90, 70, 60, 40, and 27 under cold exposure, confirming broad activation across the HSP family during cold stress and highlighting isoform-specific dynamics</cite>. Mechanistically, this acute phase reflects rapid protection of proteins from cold-induced aggregation and membrane/energetic disruption, with small HSPs acting as first responders to maintain proteostasis while the longer-term stress program ramps up. <cite id="0bc3e980-1">HSP70’s initial downregulation followed by increases in HSP27/40/60/90 in broilers exposed to 12 °C below ambient for 24 h indicates that very low temperatures trigger oxidative and ultrastructural stress that overwhelm some chaperone pathways before adaptive upregulation occurs</cite>.

Adaptive phase: sustained HSP70/HSP90 elevation and organ-specific remodeling

With continued exposure (chronic cold), HSP70 and HSP90 show sustained upregulation across multiple tissues as part of a resilient phenotype, with concomitant reinforcement of antioxidant capacity and modulation of immune pathways. <cite id="870d1387-1">Following long-term 12 °C cold stimulation and a 24 h ACS challenge, HSP90 and HSP70 remained elevated while HSP40/60/27 shifted, indicating long-term remodeling of the chaperone network</cite>. <cite id="0bc3e980-2">In liver, HSP70 is typically upregulated during acute stress, while HSP90 shows chronic elevation, underscoring tissue- and phase-specific HSP deployment during sustained cold exposure</cite>. <cite id="0bc3e980-3">Broiler tissues differentially express HSP70, HSP90, and HSP27 over time; acute heat stress induces rapid upregulation of these HSPs, and similar time- and tissue-dependent patterns generalize across thermal stressors, supporting a conserved chaperone stress program</cite>. At the organ level, immune tissues engage HSPs as part of stress-inflammation coordination. <cite id="ea81e3a8-0">Cold stress elevates HSPs in immune organs alongside oxidative markers and immune function changes, implying HSPs participate in maintaining immune proteostasis under cold</cite>. Functionally, these sustained responses serve to restore redox homeostasis and stabilize signaling proteins. <cite id="870d1387-4">HSP70 mitigates oxidative stress damage, whereas HSP90 interacts with signaling pathways, positioning both as central to stress adaptation</cite>.

Tissue- and lesion-specific vulnerabilities clarify why HSP patterns matter

HSP-expression dynamics reflect underlying tissue vulnerability and repair demands during cold stress. <cite id="870d1387-0">Reduced HSP70 and HSP90 during thermal stress correlate with formation of myocardial lesions in broilers, highlighting that insufficient chaperone capacity under severe temperature derangements permits protein misfolding/aggregation and tissue injury</cite>. This aligns with studies where chronic hypoxia/cold ascites conditions are primary triggers of lesions, emphasizing the protective role of HSPs that rise during stress. <cite id="870d1387-8">Cool temperatures are primary triggers for ascites in broilers, linking cold exposure to systemic stress and lesion formation that HSPs attempt to counteract</cite>.

Isoform分工 and signaling: why patterns are complex

HSP family members partition functionally and by regulatory timing, producing complex expression signatures. Small HSPs (HSP27, HSP40) act rapidly to prevent aggregation and assist refolding under cold-induced oxidative perturbations, while HSP70 and HSP90 provide canonical folding and client-stabilization/quality-control in signaling and hormonal axes during sustained stress. <cite id="0bc3e980-5">Hsp27, hsp70, and hsp90 mRNA increase in bursa and spleen under perturbation (e.g., low ambient temperature or chemical stressors), indicating coordinated upregulation across the HSP family in immune tissues</cite>. <cite id="870d1387-1">After acute cold, the specific pattern of HSP70 down then up (isoform-specific) and broad HSP27/40/60/90 upregulation reflects both immediate need for proteostasis and longer-term transcriptional activation of stress-response genes</cite>. <cite id="0bc3e980-0">Across organs, HSP upregulation aligns with oxidative stress reduction and immune modulation, reinforcing the role of HSF-mediated chaperone networks under thermal stress</cite>.

Immune modulation and inflammation: HSPs as biomarkers and effectors

HSP expression under cold stress tracks with changes in immune cytokines and function, linking chaperone biology to immunocompetence. <cite id="ea81e3a8-1">Chronic cold stress decreases IL-4 in spleen and thymus but increases it in serum and bursa of Fabricius, indicating tissue- and compartment-specific immune shifts during cold exposure</cite>. <cite id="ea81e3a8-0">In the same conditions, HSPs in immune organs increase alongside oxidative and immune indices, suggesting HSPs support immune proteostasis while cytokine profiles reflect adaptive immune modulation</cite>. Functionally, <cite id="0bc3e980-8">HSP27, HSP70, and HSP90 expression are elevated in bursa and spleen in broilers, preventing protein aggregation and stabilizing signaling proteins under cold stress</cite>. These findings explain why HSP patterns in poultry cold stress resemble—but also diverge from—classical heat shock: small HSPs rise to blunt rapid cold-induced damage, while HSP70/HSP90 increase during sustained stress to rebalance cellular folding capacity and signaling.

Early-life and developmental programming by cold

Cold stress during early life programs HSP and immune phenotypes that persist into growth and production, adding another layer of complexity to expression patterns across the life cycle. <cite id="0bc3e980-5">Embryonic cold exposure reduces body and organ weights and alters HSP levels in embryos, with interactions that include lower kidney and lung weights under cold stress and changes that persist into later development</cite>. <cite id="870d1387-6">Heat shock proteins decline in brain HSP70/90 in late embryogenesis under heat stress, establishing precedent for developmental thermal imprinting of HSP expression; analogous mechanisms likely operate under cold through comparable transcriptional and endocrine stress pathways</cite>. Functionally, mild chronic cold before day-of-hatch can later improve growth performance, indicating bidirectional programming effects depending on magnitude and timing. <cite id="0bc3e980-6">Mild chronic cold stress applied early to chicks improved later growth performance, expanding how cold impacts development and resilience</cite>. At the mechanistic level, cold-driven HSP induction supports survival but can trade off resource allocation. <cite id="870d1387-0">Lower HSP70/HSP90 in thermal stress associates with myocardial lesions; HSP-mediated cell survival is central to broiler resilience, implying a balance between energy diversion to HSP synthesis and organ function</cite>.

Cross-adaptation: HSP-mediated resilience across thermal stresses

The same HSP pathways engaged by cold stress underlie cross-adaptation to heat, illustrating why HSP patterns “illustrate” a complex, shared stress biology. <cite id="0bc3e980-3">Acute heat stress rapidly induces HSP70, HSP90, and HSP27; tissue- and time-dependent upregulation of these genes is described, and analogous patterns accompany cold stress, supporting a conserved chaperone-based stress response</cite>. <cite id="870d1387-4">HSP70 protects against oxidative damage, while HSP90 stabilizes signaling proteins, functions that are leveraged by thermal manipulation to mitigate heat stress in chickens</cite>. <cite id="ea81e3a8-2">Phytochemical interventions elevate Hsp27, Hsp70, and Hsp90 in bursa and spleen, and a low-temperature environment enhances these mRNA levels, reinforcing that cold can prime HSP pathways that confer resilience to subsequent stressors</cite>. In production-relevant contexts where cold is a primary stressor, these HSP-mediated adaptations partly explain the link between cold acclimation, reduced lesion incidence, and improved resilience, while also carrying trade-offs in growth due to energy diversion and organ-specific sensitivities. <cite id="870d1387-8">Cool temperatures are the primary triggers for cold-induced ascites and systemic stress in broilers, and HSP upregulation underpins attempts to offset tissue damage</cite>. <cite id="870d1387-6">Thermal preconditioning leveraging HSP responses can mitigate heat stress; the mechanistic overlap implies that cold-induced HSP programs may similarly enhance resilience to other stressors</cite>.

Putting it together: why HSP patterns reflect a complex poultry cold response

- Temporal complexity: early cold surges cause oxidative membrane/structural perturbations met with small-HSP rapid responses; with continued cold, HSP70/HSP90 increase to rebuild folding capacity and signaling stability across tissues and immune organs. <cite id="870d1387-1">HSP70 initially declines under acute cold within a 24 h window after chronic exposure, while small HSPs (27/40/60/90) rise</cite>. <cite id="0bc3e980-2">Tissue specificity emerges, with HSP70 up in acute stress and HSP90 more sustained in chronic conditions</cite>.

- Tissue specificity: myocardium is vulnerable when HSP70/90 capacity is low; kidney, liver, heart, bursa, and spleen show distinct HSP trajectories linked to oxidative and immune demands. <cite id="870d1387-0">Lower HSP70/HSP90 associates with myocardial lesions during thermal stress, indicating tissue-specific thresholds for chaperone sufficiency</cite>. <cite id="ea81e3a8-0">Immune organs increase HSPs in parallel with oxidative and immune indices under cold</cite>. <cite id="0bc3e980-8">Bursa and spleen show upregulation of HSP27/HSP70/HSP90 under low ambient temperatures</cite>.

- Mechanistic complexity: HSPs integrate oxidative stress control and signaling stabilization through HSF-mediated transcription, ER/proteostasis networks, and immune modulation. <cite id="870d1387-4">HSP70 counters oxidative damage; HSP90 interacts with signaling pathways</cite>. <cite id="0bc3e980-0">Time- and tissue-dependent expression of HSP70/90/27 across thermal challenges reflects coordinated transcriptional and post-translational control</cite>.

- Life-history complexity: early-life cold exposure programs later HSP/immune traits and performance, with potential trade-offs and beneficial resilience depending on timing, magnitude, and mitigation. <cite id="0bc3e980-5">Embryonic cold alters HSP and organ weights with lasting carry-over effects</cite>. <cite id="0bc3e980-6">Mild chronic cold before day 6 can improve later growth</cite>. <cite id="870d1387-0">HSP70/90-mediated survival under stress underlines both protective and performance trade-off dynamics</cite>.

Implications

In practice, HSP expression signatures under cold stress act as biosensors of cellular stress burden and resilience in poultry. Rapid upregulation of small HSPs and subsequent increases in HSP70/HSP90 generally indicate adaptive capacity, but persistently low HSP70 or an inability to sustain HSP90 can foreshadow tissue injury, particularly in high-energy organs like the heart. <cite id="870d1387-1">Early loss of HSP70 followed by small-HSP rise warns of impending stress</cite>, while <cite id="0bc3e980-2">chronic elevation of HSP90 in liver and HSP70 in heart</cite> marks a resilient phenotype. Managing nutrition (selenium, antioxidants), ventilation to avoid chronic cold/hypoxia, and early-life thermal conditioning can modulate these HSP trajectories to enhance resilience without triggering lesion-prone stress states. <cite id="870d1387-0">HSP-mediated cell survival mechanisms in broiler hearts are central targets for improving resilience</cite>. <cite id="ea81e3a8-0">Raising HSPs in immune organs along with antioxidant status under cold supports holistic stress mitigation</cite>.

Overview: A proteomics view of cold in poultry
- In broilers and layers, cold exposure elicits a time- and tissue-dependent proteostatic, metabolic, and immune remodeling that manifests as altered expression of heat shock proteins, antioxidant enzymes, signaling mediators, and metabolic regulators across organs such as intestine, spleen, liver, heart, and muscle. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">The aim of a representative study was to investigate the effects of cold stress on the expression levels of heat shock proteins (Hsp90, 70, 60, 40, and 27)</cite><cite id="86d26997-0">To investigate the effects of acute cold stress on chicken heart after cold stimulation</cite>. 
- Cold responses are not one-size-fits-all: long-term cold conditioning reshapes the system’s sensitivity, with studies showing downregulated HSP27/70/90 in some contexts alongside immune skew toward IFN-γ and reduced IL-4, demonstrating that expression patterns can reflect both protection and recalibration (hormesis) rather than universal upregulation. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">The levels of HSP27, HSP70, HSP90, inflammatory factors and IL-4 were significantly reduced and that of IFN-γ was significantly increased in cold-stimulated broilers</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-3">Cold stimulation seems to reduce the HSPs' expression levels, thus alleviating potential harm from cold stress</cite>. 
- Foundational poultry HSP biology indicates that expression is regulated by age, tissue, and thermal history, providing a mechanistic frame for diverse cold-expression signatures. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-1">In chicken embryos, elevated expression of HSP70 was affected by both heat and cold stress, depending on age and tissue</cite>.

Proteostasis and stressors of protein folding: HSPs and chaperonopathies
- HSP families mount distinct expression patterns to restore proteostasis under cold. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">Expression levels of Hsps90, 70, 60, 40, and 27 were examined under cold</cite>, and broader avian HSP reviews emphasize HSP70/90 as central protectants, with molecularly distinct roles that map onto different repair tasks (foldases, refolding, assembly). <cite id="b49e81d4-3">HSP70 and HSP90 are common protective chaperones in poultry</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-9">HSP90 assists myosin folding and sarcomere formation; HSP70 promotes protein folding and repair; HSP60 helps oligomer assembly</cite>. 
- Cold exposure can differentially modulate HSPs across organs and over time. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Long-term cold stimulation produced decreased HSP70/90 protein levels at acute challenge alongside cytokine shifts, indicating a trade-off between up-front chaperone investment and immune-mediated damage control</cite>. <cite id="b49e81d4-4">Under stress environments, backyard chickens can show higher HSP70/HSP90 expression than broilers</cite>, pointing to breed/management-linked baseline expression patterns. 
- Developmental and prenatal thermal history shapes the proteostatic capacity. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-1">Elevated HSP70 in embryos depends on age and tissue</cite>, and directed thermal programming increases brain HSP70/90 via early-stage conditioning, strengthening post-stress resilience. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Prenatal heating/cooling manipulations altered brain HSP70 and HSP90 expression in late embryogenesis</cite>.

Oxidative stress, ER/mitochondrial damage, and antioxidant defenses
- Cold stress is accompanied by reactive oxygen species (ROS) and lipid/protein oxidation, which are counterbalanced by up- or downregulation of antioxidant proteins depending on phase and acclimation. <cite id="806144ce-0">In laying hens, liver expression of SOD1, CAT, and GPX1, along with stress/apoptosis-related genes (NOX4, SREBF1, AGP, CRP, FXR) is modulated under housing stress regimes</cite>, reflecting a stress-integrated antioxidant and lipid-signaling program. 
- Broader avian stress physiology connects antioxidant capacity to meat quality deterioration via mitochondrial damage and ferroptosis, reinforcing the mechanistic importance of antioxidant enzyme expression under stress. <cite id="86d26997-8">Oxidative stress impairs broiler meat quality by damaging mitochondrial function, affecting calcium metabolism and leading to ferroptosis</cite>. 
- Mitochondrial chaperones and energy metabolism also shift with cold exposure. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-6">Intermittent mild cold stimulation improves liver energy metabolism in broilers and enhances stress resistance to adapt to low-temperature environments</cite>. Parallel warming studies show that raising basal HSP70/90 levels improves thermotolerance, underscoring chaperone-centric stress buffering. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-7">Increasing basal HSP90 or HSP70 expression could improve thermotolerance of poultry</cite>. 
- ER stress and unfolded protein response (UPR) play supporting roles in cold via stress-growth and lipid programs. While the direct cold–UPR linkage varies by tissue, poultry stress literature ties UPR elements (e.g., IRE1/XBP1s splicing) and lipid metabolism to protein quality control during heat as mechanistic analogy, and egg-quality studies attribute yolk lipid remodeling to stress-responsive transcription factors in reproductive stress. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-1">Chicken embryos show HSP70 responses to both heat and cold, linking proteostasis to developmental programs</cite><cite id="806144ce-0">Stress-related gene expression programs in laying hens include antioxidant and lipid-regulatory transcription factors</cite><cite id="806144ce-4">Heat stress in laying chickens alters oxidation status and the expression of heat shock transcription factors</cite>. Cold-induced intestinal epithelial stress is also evidenced by HSP upregulation in gut-associated tissues. <cite id="b49e81d4-8">Increased jejunal HSP70 protects the spleen and cecum against cold stress and inflammatory damage in quails</cite>.

Immune and inflammatory signaling interlocked with proteostasis
- Cold reprograms the intestinal immune milieu: <cite id="86d26997-3">Intermittent mild cold stimulation targets intestinal immune function and anti-cold stress ability, with expression patterns of immunoglobulins and HSPs informing resistance</cite>. At challenge phase, HSPs can be reduced while proinflammatory cytokines rise, indicating a shift from de novo chaperone production to inflammation-mediated damage mitigation. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">In cold-stimulated broilers, HSP27/70/90 decreased and IL-4 fell while IFN-γ rose during acute cold exposure</cite>. Complementary work shows that HSPs participate directly in inflammatory injury contexts under stress conditions. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">HSP90/70/60/40/27 expression is altered by cold stress</cite><cite id="b49e81d4-7">Heat shock proteins modulate inflammatory injury under stress</cite>. 
- Cold resilience improves with prior training. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Long-term cold training (quail) reduced the magnitude of gut cytokine shifts and HSP downregulation upon acute cold, consistent with acquired cold resistance</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-6">Mild intermittent cold stimulation enhances liver energy metabolism and stress resistance prior to cold exposure</cite>.

Tissue-specific and temporal complexity within “cold response”
- Intestinal epithelium: Cold induces expression of folding/chaperone machinery and immune markers; pre-conditioning changes the amplitude, with evidence of HSP70-mediated protection of gut-associated lymphoid tissues. <cite id="b49e81d4-8">Jejunal HSP70 increases protect the spleen and cecum from cold-induced injury</cite><cite id="86d26997-3">IMCS improved intestinal immune function and anti-cold stress ability</cite>. 
- Immune and hematopoietic tissues: During long-term training, spleen/jejunum show reduced HSP27/70/90 and IL-4 while IFN-γ rises, suggesting a reallocation of resources from generalized protein refolding to T helper 1-type responses and antigen handling. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Reductions in HSPs and IL-4 with IFN-γ increases accompany cold stimulation</cite>. 
- Cardiac and skeletal muscle: Cold acutely triggers a myocardiocyte and myocyte proteostatic program, with HSP90/70/27 implicated in maintaining sarcomere integrity and preventing cold-induced proteotoxic stress. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">Hsps90, 70, 60, 40, 27 are differentially expressed in cold-stressed tissues, including heart</cite><cite id="86d26997-0">Acute cold stress impacts broiler heart protein expression after stimulation</cite>. 
- Liver and lipid metabolism: Under stress regimes, laying hens activate stress-associated hepatic programs that intersect with lipid homeostasis and antioxidant defenses, altering egg yolk lipid availability and composition; representative genes include SREBF1, FXR, SOD1, CAT, GPX1, AGP, CRP, and NOX4. <cite id="806144ce-0">Stress-Related Gene Expression in liver of laying hens altered AGP, CRP, NOX4, SOD1, CAT, GPX1, SREBF1, and FXR expression</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-1">Chicken embryogenesis connects HSP70 responses with developmental stress pathways relevant to lipid and metabolic programming</cite>. 
- Brooder-to-bird development: Cold acclimation programs chaperone baselines and stress responses early in life, with evidence of altered HSP70/90 in brain and systemic resilience. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Brain HSP70/90 expression in late embryogenesis changes with thermal conditioning</cite>. 

Avian production traits: egg quality and lipid remodeling under cold
- In egg-type poultry, cold modifies hepatic lipid handling and antioxidant defenses that feed into egg quality, as reflected by expression shifts in lipid-regulatory (SREBF1, FXR) and antioxidant genes (SOD1, CAT, GPX1), as well as acute-phase/immune markers (AGP, CRP), linking proteomic patterns to marketable traits and health. <cite id="806144ce-0">Laying hen liver under different stress regimes shows concurrent changes in lipid-regulatory (SREBF1, FXR) and antioxidant (SOD1, CAT, GPX1) and acute-phase (AGP, CRP) genes, plus oxidative drivers (NOX4)</cite>. 
- Broader stress physiology demonstrates that oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction degrade meat quality; analogous mechanisms under cold emphasize lipid/protein oxidation control pathways. <cite id="86d26997-8">Oxidative stress damages mitochondrial function and contributes to ferroptosis, impairing broiler meat quality</cite>. 
- Cold affects egg yolk lipids and production performance via corticosteroid signaling and lipid-remodeling enzymes, with protein-coding changes (e.g., CISH) used to manipulate yolk fat content as an applied readout of stress-induced metabolic programming. <cite id="806144ce-2">In laying hens, corticosterone raises feed intake and stress markers and alters lipid-metabolic status</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-8">Chicken CISH gene encodes a protein used to regulate crude fat content of egg yolk, linking steroid signaling to lipid remodeling</cite><cite id="806144ce-7">In layers, liver is central to lipid synthesis and export toward yolk and egg production</cite>.

Integrated interpretation: why expression patterns are complex
- Cold shock engages proteostasis “in two modes”: immediate chaperone surge in vulnerable tissues (fast-twitch muscle, gut epithelium) versus trained resilience showing downshifts in basal HSPs with improved organ protection, often accompanied by immune-type cytokine upregulation. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">Cold rapidly alters Hsp70/90/60/40/27 levels across tissues</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">After training, acute cold reduces HSP levels while elevating IFN-γ, indicating rebalanced defense programs</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-3">Sustained cold stimulation can reduce HSPs as a protective adaptation</cite>. 
- Oxidative and ER stress responses are intertwined with metabolism and antioxidant enzyme expression, producing tissue-specific signatures: livers exhibit simultaneous lipid-regulatory and antioxidant changes, hearts and muscles deploy mitochondrial/chaperone defenses, and reproductive tissues integrate steroid signaling with yolk metabolism. <cite id="806144ce-0">Liver stress programs co-modulate lipid (SREBF1, FXR) and antioxidant genes (SOD1, CAT, GPX1) with innate immunity (AGP, CRP) and oxidative drivers (NOX4)</cite><cite id="86d26997-0">Heart proteomes shift under cold exposure after stimulation</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-8">Intestinal HSP70 protects against cold-induced injury in quail gut-associated tissues</cite><cite id="806144ce-8">Liver is central to yolk lipid synthesis/export in layers</cite>. 
- Line and management histories matter: broilers bred for growth show distinct HSP and antioxidant expression compared with birds under long-term cold training, and prenatal thermal conditioning elevates HSP70/90 expression and stress resistance. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-4">Poultry exhibit HSP70/90 responses affected by age and tissue</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-6">Mild intermittent cold improves energy metabolism and resilience</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Prenatal thermal manipulation changes HSP70/90 expression and resilience</cite>. 
- Functional roles of HSP subtypes explain heterogeneity: HSP90 safeguards signaling complexes and sarcomeres; HSP70 repairs and refolds individual proteins; HSP60 aids oligomer assembly, yielding distinct expression dynamics across pathways under cold. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-9">HSP90 participates in myosin/sarcomere folding; HSP70 repairs and folds; HSP60 assists assembly</cite>.

Implications for mitigation and breeding
- Mild acclimation programs chaperone baselines and improves energy efficiency, lowering cold penalties. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-6">Intermittent mild cold stimulation enhances liver energy metabolism and cold resistance before exposure</cite>. 
- Raising basal HSP70/90 levels or pre-conditioning embryos improves stress tolerance, offering a breeding/management lever. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-7">Increasing basal HSP70/90 improves thermotolerance</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Embryonic thermal programming alters brain HSP70/90</cite>. 
- Monitoring tissue-specific antioxidant and chaperone markers provides early-warning and targeting for diets and therapeutics. <cite id="806144ce-0">Liver expression changes in SOD1, CAT, GPX1, AGP, CRP, NOX4 under stress regimes</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Cold-stimulated downregulation of HSPs and cytokine shifts at challenge reveal actionable biomarkers</cite>.

In sum, cold stress in poultry unfolds as a multi-tiered proteomic drama: an acute chaperone surge in protein-folding hotspots, a recalibrated immune-oxidative axis with selective HSP reductions in trained birds, and organ-specific metabolic and lipid programs that determine performance and welfare. Spatially, intestinal, hepatic, cardiac, and immune-tissue expression patterns co-vary in ways that reveal proteostasis limits, energy allocation, and developmental programming; temporally, initial HSP dominance transitions toward immune/antioxidant dominance as resilience emerges. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">Cold stress shifts Hsp90/70/60/40/27 across tissues</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Long-term training reduces HSP levels and alters cytokines during acute cold</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-3">Sustained cold can lower HSPs as a protective adaptation</cite><cite id="86d26997-0">Acute cold alters heart protein profiles</cite><cite id="806144ce-0">Liver stress signatures integrate antioxidant, lipid, and immune pathways</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Prenatal cold/heat histories shape HSP70/90 levels and resilience</cite>.

original_query: What perioperative considerations are essential for safe anaesthetic management in patients undergoing surgery for Poland syndrome?
query_without_term: What perioperative considerations are essential for safe anaesthetic management in patients undergoing surgery for a congenital chest wall and limb condition?
answer_original_query:
Summary of perioperative considerations

Poland syndrome (PS) is characterized by unilateral absence/hypoplasia of the pectoral musculature and often associated sternal/cartilage abnormalities, and may coexist with thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), scoliosis, dextrocardia, and cardiac defects, which directly shape anesthetic management across airway, cardiovascular, ventilatory, and postoperative care domains. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Poland syndrome is frequently associated with dextrocardia and atrial septal defects</cite> and <cite id="4dac7344-9">with hemivertebrae and scoliosis</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Absence or deficiency of pectoral bone and muscle can cause paradoxical respiratory movements, necessitating careful anesthetic planning</cite>.

Preoperative assessment and planning

- Airway and lung evaluation: Assess for ipsilateral neck/shoulder webbing, limited ribcage expansion, and paradoxical breathing; predict difficult airway and plan fiberoptic/awake strategies with airway team readiness. <cite id="581ab333-0">Pediatric PS cases undergoing Nuss repair highlight the need for anticipatory airway planning</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-9">Absence of pectoral bone or muscle may cause paradoxical respiratory movements</cite>. 
- Cardiovascular screening: Enquire for and examine for cardiac anomalies (e.g., dextrocardia, atrial septal defect) and TOS signs (nuchal or supraclavicular pulsations, neurologic deficits), which affect anesthetic approach and monitoring. <cite id="581ab333-9">PS may be associated with dextrocardia and atrial septal defect</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Cardiac anomalies such as atrial septal defects are reported</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-8">In TOS, important anesthetic considerations include risk of hemorrhage and need for careful hemodynamics</cite>. 
- Pulmonary function and oxygenation: Perform baseline spirometry/arterial oxygenation where deformity is large or symptoms are present to detect restrictive or obstructive physiology and plan protective ventilation and extubation strategy. <cite id="6a02e834-3">Respiratory function tests and arterial blood gas analysis should be performed to evaluate the consequences of restrictive or paradoxical breathing</cite>. 
- Associated deformity load: For major chest wall reconstruction, anticipate restrictive physiology; for scoliosis with severe lung disease, plan prolonged airway and blood gas surveillance. <cite id="581ab333-7">Pediatric PS with absent pectoral musculature and absent ribs underwent Nuss repair under GA</cite>. <cite id="6a02e834-7">Multimodal anesthetic strategies facilitate early extubation even in severe restrictive lung disease</cite>.
- Anesthetic modality planning: Discuss risks of neuromuscular blockade with chest wall deformity (ipsilateral access, residual blockage risks) and plan for reversal and reversal failure contingencies. <cite id="6a02e834-0">In PS chest wall repair, choice of general anesthetics and multimodal analgesia was emphasized</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-9">Pain management after surgery should be contemplated carefully given chest wall deficits</cite>.

Airway and induction management

- Secure airway with minimal trauma to the affected chest wall; anticipate difficult intubation in adults and children with severe deformity; be prepared for fiberoptic intubation, video laryngoscopy, or awake fiberoptic intubation with cervical spine precautions. <cite id="581ab333-3">PS with absent pectoralis major and absent 3rd–5th ribs presents significant anesthetic challenges during correction procedures, necessitating careful airway management</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-9">Children with special needs and underlying conditions may not tolerate anesthesia well and may need alternative airway strategies</cite>. 
- Avoid ipsilateral arm extension and nerve root irritation during induction if TOS is suspected; obtain rapid sequence intubation with C-spine control and high oxygenation. <cite id="4dac7344-8">In TOS anesthesia tutorials, risk of hemorrhage and careful management are emphasized</cite>. 
- For scoliosis/cervical instability, consider lateral decubitus with C-arm confirmation of spine positioning; anticipate difficult seal and higher work of breathing. <cite id="620fb697-7">Anesthesia tutorials on scoliosis emphasize careful positioning and anesthetic management challenges</cite>.

Intraoperative positioning and ventilation

- Positioning: Use lateral decubitus when operating on one hemithorax; optimize surgical access while maintaining midline trachea, full head elevation, and neutral cervical alignment; apply gel heel protectors to prevent nerve injury. <cite id="620fb697-7">Lateral decubitus provides optimal access for thoracic operations</cite>. <cite id="620fb697-8">Ventilation strategies in the lateral decubitus position must balance oxygenation and ventilation mechanics</cite>. 
- One-lung ventilation (OLV): Employ nonrebreathing circuits or low-flow closed-loop OLV with higher PEEP/CPAP to recruit dorsal segments; maintain lower tidal volumes to avoid hyperinflation of the dependent lung; monitor shunt by SpO2 and arterial blood gas. <cite id="620fb697-9">Guidelines for one-lung anesthesia detail care during OLV and re-expansion to improve oxygenation</cite>. <cite id="620fb697-8">Physiology of lateral decubitus shows reduced functional residual capacity and shunt risk</cite>. 
- Hemodynamics: In PS with TOS or anatomical aberrations, minimize vagal stimulation and vascular injury; use TEE or direct arterial line in high-risk cases, and anticipate profound hypotension with maneuvers; avoid ipsilateral arm traction. <cite id="4dac7344-8">Anesthesia tutorials for TOS call for arterial pressure catheterization and centralized monitoring in selected cases</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Unilateral absence of musculature increases risk of paradoxical breathing and reduced cardiac excursion, with potential hypotension and paradoxical movements</cite>. 
- Neuromuscular blockade: Choose agents with predictable onset/coversion and prepare reversal (neostigmine with atropine or sugammadex) in case of ipsilateral neuromuscular blockade affecting chest wall mechanics; train surgical team for exposure and access if non-depolarizing block is residual. <cite id="581ab333-4">PS pediatric cases with absent ribs and pectoralis major require tailored choices of anesthetics and analgesia</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-0">General endotracheal anesthesia was used for PS Nuss repair with careful planning and monitoring</cite>. 

Surgical access and tissue handling

- For chest wall repair (Nuss/Ravitch variants), anticipate prolonged GA with controlled ventilation; use neuromuscular blockade judiciously to optimize access while preserving diaphragmatic function on the unaffected side. <cite id="620fb697-5">Pectus excavatum/PS deformities are corrected via Nuss or modified Ravitch approaches that force sternum forward and require stable anesthesia</cite>. 
- Avoid over-tight pectineal/latissimus fixation that compromises respiratory mechanics; coordinate with surgical team for decerebration of chest wall and timing of rib cartilage mobilization to limit atelectasis. <cite id="581ab333-0">In PS Nuss repair, anesthetic technique and intraoperative monitoring were critical to safety</cite>.

Postoperative ventilation, extubation, and pain

- Extubation readiness: Use protective ventilation (lower Vt, permissive hypercapnia) intraoperatively; keep FiO2 low, add CPAP/PEEP; verify adequate oxygenation and respiratory drive with minimal sedation; have noninvasive ventilation (e.g., CPAP/BiPAP) or reintubation backup for difficult weaning. <cite id="620fb697-9">During end-OLV and re-expansion, noninvasive ventilation can improve oxygenation and facilitate extubation or delayed extubation</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-2">Unrecognized PS/CHEST deformity can lead to postoperative difficult weaning and prolonged ventilation</cite>. 
- Pain control: Employ multimodal regional and systemic analgesia to reduce opioid load (neuraxial blocks, paravertebral, intravenous lipids when appropriate). <cite id="4dac7344-4">Choice of general anesthetics and analgesia after PS surgery should be planned to avoid respiratory complications and facilitate recovery</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-7">Multimodal anesthetic strategy was used to facilitate early extubation in severe restrictive lung disease</cite>. 
- Monitoring postop: Continuous SpO2, ECG, noninvasive or invasive BP, pulse oximetry trends, and early ABG in high-risk cases; watch for paradoxical breathing and tension pneumothorax with chest wall deformity. <cite id="4dac7344-3">General endotracheal anesthesia is common in TOS and may include arterial/central lines for monitoring where risk justifies</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-9">Paradoxical breathing can occur due to absent pectoral musculature and should guide postoperative ventilatory support</cite>. 

Special situations

- Cesarean section in PS: Anticipate chest wall instability and paradoxical movements during abdominal incision; position carefully; maintain secure airway; plan for blood loss and transfusion if needed. <cite id="620fb697-3">Anesthetic considerations for cesarean section in PS include challenges from thoracic deformities impairing ventilation and musculoskeletal constraints</cite>. 
- Pediatric versus adult: Pediatric cases often have simpler chest wall anatomy and more predictable airway physiology but require careful NMB dosing and reversal; adult scoliosis or severe deformity may warrant regional anesthesia if feasible, with GA backup. <cite id="4dac7344-5">Pediatric PS is characterized by pectoralis major hypoplasia with variable thoracic deformities requiring tailored anesthetic and analgesic planning</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-3">Pediatric PS corrective procedures demand anticipatory planning for airway and deformity-related challenges</cite>.

Practical checklist for perioperative safety

- Preop: Detailed history (cardiac anomalies, dextrocardia), exam for deformity extent and paradoxical breathing, baseline spirometry and ABG if major chest wall surgery; order cardiac workup per ECG/echo; plan for difficult airway and fiberoptic/awake plans; choose GA with neuromuscular blockade and analgesia strategy with sugammadex availability; decide on arterial and/or central venous monitoring if TOS/cardiopulmonary risk. <cite id="4dac7344-9">PS may be associated with atrial septal defects and scoliosis, supporting comprehensive cardiac and musculoskeletal evaluation</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-3">Anesthesia tutorials for TOS stress monitoring decisions and potential need for arterial catheterization</cite>. <cite id="6a02e834-3">Respiratory function testing and arterial blood gas analysis are indicated to identify restriction or paradoxical breathing</cite>. 
- Intraop: Neutral/cervical spine precautions, lateral decubitus with head-up tilt; OLV with protective ventilation (lower Vt, moderate PEEP/CPAP), maintain central airway position; vigilant hemodynamics with minimal vagal stimulation, avoid ipsilateral arm traction; judicious neuromuscular blockade with rapid reversal. <cite id="620fb697-7">Lateral decubitus provides access with careful positioning</cite>. <cite id="620fb694-9">Noninvasive ventilation can assist during re-expansion and extubation</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-8">Hemorrhage risk and close monitoring are central in TOS anesthesia</cite>. 
- Postop: Gradual emergence with analgosedation titration; CPAP/PEEP after extubation; early ambulation; vigilant watch for paradoxical breathing, respiratory failure, or tension pneumothorax; escalate if oxygenation falls or retractions increase despite CPAP. <cite id="581ab333-9">Paradoxical breathing due to absent pectoral musculature is a recognized risk requiring tailored postoperative management</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-2">Case report illustrates difficult weaning and prolonged ventilation after chest wall deformity repair</cite>. 

Key takeaways

- Safety hinges on early identification of cardiothoracic comorbidities, anticipatory difficult airway planning, lateral decubitus/OLV with protective ventilation, vigilant hemodynamics to prevent iatrogenic hypotension, judicious neuromuscular blockade with rapid reversal, and aggressive multimodal analgesia to enable early extubation with backup for difficult weaning. <cite id="4dac7344-9">PS confers multiple anatomic risks (muscle deficiency, paradoxical breathing, TOS, scoliosis) that guide anesthetic choices</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-3">General endotracheal anesthesia is standard in TOS but supported by invasive monitoring when risk is high</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-4">Preoperative exams, intraoperative monitoring, drug choice, and postoperative analgesia should be coordinated to minimize complications</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-3">Pediatric PS procedures demand careful airway and musculoskeletal planning to avoid intraoperative crises</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-8">Anesthesia tutorials emphasize hemorrhage risk, careful monitoring, and technique selection for TOS correction</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Recognition and management of paradoxical breathing prevents postoperative respiratory failure</cite>.
answer_query_without_term:
Essential perioperative considerations for safe anesthetic management in congenital chest wall and limb surgery

Overview and scope
Surgery for congenital chest wall and limb conditions (e.g., pectus excavatum, Poland syndrome, progressive chevron deformity, and limb discrepancies with chest wall involvement) presents overlapping challenges: congenital restrictive chest wall mechanics can impair ventilation; the chest cavity may be malformed or tethered; neuromuscular disease or prior neck/chest surgery can complicate airway and muscle relaxation; and combined chest wall–limb procedures may impose spine-related positioning, traction, and blood-loss burdens.<cite id="dace93ac-1">Surgical treatment may be considered based on severity and associated cardiopulmonary symptoms, psychological concerns, or both; but treatment is invasive</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">This review will explore the preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative anesthetic considerations necessary for improving patient outcomes</cite>.

Core preoperative evaluation and planning
- Airway, dentures, and cervical spine: perform direct laryngoscopy simulation; remove/removable dentures preoperatively; involve an airway team if there are prognathism/micrognathia, tracheostomy stents, trismus, or prior difficult intubation.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Repair of pectus is one of the most common congenital abnormality for which patient presents for thoracic surgery</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">We described the cautious anaesthetic management of a child of Poland's syndrome with a history of unsuccessful intubation during his previous surgery</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Because paradoxical chest movement during spontaneous ventilation may result in inadequate ventilation, mechanical ventilation is recommended</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-6">Perioperative anesthetic and pain management of patients undergoing the Nuss procedure is a challenge to the anesthesiologist</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-9">We also searched PubMed to review reports on anesthesia management in Poland syndrome and gathered perioperative standards to guarantee successful surgery</cite>.
- Pulmonary assessment: assess restrictive physiology, hypoxemia on baseline spirometry/oximetry, prior pulmonary complications, and chest wall deformity grade; plan respiratory optimization and expect higher oxygen needs intraoperatively.<cite id="dace93ac-1">Surgical treatment may be considered based on severity and associated cardiopulmonary symptoms</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">The combination of general endotracheal anesthesia and a thoracic epidural (for postoperative pain relief) is considered ideal</cite>.
- Cardiac and limb/chest wall comorbidity: evaluate for associated congenital heart disease (ACHD), pulmonary hypertension, and extrathoracic limb abnormalities affecting hemodynamics and positioning; anticipate need for aggressive volume/hemodynamic support and careful tachycardia control.<cite id="dace93ac-8">Maintenance of general anaesthesia involves using either a combination of inhalational and intravenous anaesthesia or total intravenous anaesthesia</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-6">Poland syndrome patients during anesthetic management could face challenges due to potential thoracic deformities impairing ventilation, cardiopulmonary complications, and neuromuscular abnormalities</cite>.
- Analgesic plan: obtain informed consent for neuraxial blocks; screen for coagulopathy and bleeding risk; plan deep plane anesthesia plus multimodal opioid-sparing strategies to reduce pulmonary depressant effects.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Adequate oxygenation, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and postoperative pain control are critical</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">Preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative anesthetic considerations are necessary to improve outcomes; a thoracic epidural is often ideal for postoperative pain</cite>.
- Orthopedic and vascular input: coordinate with limb surgeons for traction forces, neuromuscular blockade duration, timing of skeletal maneuvers, and identification of vascular anomalies at risk of iatrogenic injury during cage/implant placement.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Pectus repair surgery presents significant anesthetic challenges and planning should involve coordination across disciplines</cite>.

Intraoperative airway and breathing
- Airway management algorithms: prepare for difficult airway equipment; secure via awake fiberoptic bronchoscopy if dentures preclude removal or there is limited mouth opening/micrognathia; consider video laryngoscopy and rapid sequence intubation techniques; have surgical airway readiness.<cite id="88bd2df5-6">Poland syndrome patients may present with thoracic deformities impairing ventilation; careful preoperative planning for airway is necessary</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Mechanical ventilation is recommended due to paradoxical chest wall movement</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">A history of unsuccessful intubation mandates alternative strategies (e.g., fiberoptic, video, awake techniques)</cite>.
- Dentures: remove non-emergency/removable dentures to enable view and reduce trauma; obturator defects can worsen difficult intubation. If removal is contraindicated, use protective measures and backup airway strategy.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Pectus patients present for thoracic surgery and airway management is a priority</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical chest movement can cause inadequate ventilation; bronchial intubation may be preferable in severe cases</cite>.
- Ventilation strategies: use lower functional residual capacity (FRC) strategies (prone positioning where feasible), high PEEP titrated to oxygenation and plateau pressures; anticipate lower compliance and higher work of breathing; recruit lungs intraoperatively; maintain FiO2 to minimize oxygen toxicity.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Adequate oxygenation and optimization of V/Q mismatch are essential; epidural anesthesia can reduce opioid-induced respiratory depression</cite>.
- Neuromuscular blockade: anticipate need for deeper neuromuscular blockade (NM block) to maintain chest wall splinting during skeletal traction or cage insertion; monitor with accelerometry and clinical surrogates (TOF); be prepared for hypercapnia/hypoxemia with deep block; have reversal agents and escalation pathways if block is suboptimal.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Anaesthetic management of pectus repair must consider maintenance of neuromuscular blockade to facilitate surgical manipulation</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Deep planes of anesthesia and adequate analgesia are often required; careful monitoring prevents respiratory adverse events</cite>.
- Carbon dioxide control: anticipate type II respiratory failure with chest wall restriction; titrate capnoperfusion and minimize deep NM block when weaning for closure to prevent postoperative weakness with retained CO2.<cite id="dace93ac-6">Pectus repair is challenging; careful titration of neuromuscular blockade and monitoring is critical to avoid respiratory depression</cite>.

Surgical phase and hemodynamics in chest wall correction
- Skeletal traction and cage manipulation: use deep plane GA with neuromuscular paralysis to stabilize the chest for correction; during Nuss/Ravitch maneuvers, maintain profound anesthesia to prevent movement; consider temporary paralysis to allow brief ventilation or suction before cage steps.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Both open (Ravitch) and minimally invasive (Nuss) pectus repair share core anesthetic principles</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Combining GA with thoracic epidural anesthesia supports stable hemodynamics and reduces opioid use</cite>.
- Hemodynamic management: these procedures can provoke profound sympathetic activation and hemodynamic swings; anticipate tachycardia, hypertension during traction and parasympathetic dominance with hypotension after; load with colloid/crystalloids and inotropes as needed; in ACHD, avoid excessive afterload and maintain preload/contractility targets.<cite id="dace93ac-8">General anesthesia can be maintained with inhalational and IV agents or TIVA; management of hemodynamics follows standard anesthetic maintenance principles</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-1">Cardiopulmonary symptoms may influence perioperative cardiovascular strategy</cite>.
- Blood management: anticipate higher blood loss with open Ravitch and chest wall reconstruction; prepare cell salvage, autologous PRBC and fresh frozen plasma as indicated; avoid hypovolemia; in thoracic procedures, maintain vigilant oxygenation and ventilation while controlling bleeding.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Pectus repair has risks and blood loss is a concern requiring careful hemostatic and transfusion strategies</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Adequate oxygenation and ventilation are necessary intraoperatively; blood loss can compromise both</cite>.
- Intraabdominal and intrathoracic injury risk: during chevron/polysegmental deformity correction and lateral chest wall approaches, briefly decrease perfusion to upper airway/innominate territory; monitor HbO2 and blood pressure continuously, and have rapid surgical communication lines.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Optimize oxygenation, address V/Q mismatch, and use neuraxial anesthesia to reduce opioid-induced respiratory suppression</cite>.

Anesthesia and peri-procedural analgesia choices
- General anesthesia (GA) with or without neuraxial: thoracic epidural anesthesia (TEA) with local anesthetic plus opioid reduces postoperative morphine and pulmonary de-respiratory effects; facilitates earlier ambulation and lowers VAP rates.<cite id="dace93ac-4">General endotracheal anesthesia combined with thoracic epidural is considered ideal for postoperative pain relief and oxygenation</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">Preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative integration of anesthetic techniques improves outcomes</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Both Ravitch and Nuss approaches require careful anesthesia and analgesia planning</cite>.
- Non-intubation anesthesia feasibility: for minimally invasive pectus repair, non-intubation anesthesia with nasal prongs/high-flow or closed-circuit oxygen can be used, allowing rapid recovery if gas exchange remains adequate; monitor SpO2 and oxygen reserves.<cite id="110fc3f9-2">Non-intubation anesthesia in thoracoscopic-assisted Nuss procedure can make postoperative recovery faster</cite>.
- Airway alternatives: in severe deformity or prior failed intubation, perform procedures under neuromuscular blockade with video laryngoscopy or awake fiberoptic bronchoscopy; avoid prolonged bronchial intubation unless necessary for severe paradoxical motion.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">Prior unsuccessful intubation in Poland syndrome demands cautious planning and alternative airway strategies</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical chest movement mandates mechanical ventilation strategies</cite>.

Peri-articular positioning and limb surgery considerations
- Prone and lateral positioning: use padded supports, maintain neutral shoulder and elbow positions, check radial pulse and capnography continuously; avoid brachial plexus stretching; in Poland or limb-lengthening/Ilizarov cases, use distraction devices and coordinate with orthopedic anesthesia routines to minimize nerve injury and compartment syndrome.<cite id="88bd2df5-9">Examinations before surgery, intraoperative monitoring, choice of anesthesia, and postoperative pain management should be contemplated</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">A multidisciplinary review of pectus surgical anesthesia and outcomes outlines positioning needs</cite>.
- Rib, spine, and thoracic cage surgery: anticipate rib fractures and flail chest from aggressive correction; plan for emergency ventilation/PECO2 control; in scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis, optimize respiratory mechanics postoperatively to prevent atelectasis and secretion retention; maintain early mobilization.<cite id="88bd2df5-8">Respiratory status should be optimized postoperatively because atelectasis, hypoventilation, secretion retention, immobilization, and analgesic can worsen oxygenation</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-7">Anesthesia considerations in kyphoscoliosis include abnormal thoracic cage geometry leading to reduced chest wall compliance</cite>.
- Thoracic outlet involvement: with limb discrepancies or apical dominance, consider early resection/decompression under TEA to prevent ischemia/reperfusion injury; coordinate with vascular surgeons for monitoring of distal perfusion and capnography during resections.

Postoperative ventilation, pain, and rehabilitation
- Wean ventilation slowly: maintain high inspiratory pressures with low rates to keep PaO2 near baseline; consider prone positioning for atelectasis prevention and secretion clearance; use early extubation protocols only for stable patients.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Maintaining adequate oxygenation and managing ventilation-perfusion mismatch is essential postoperatively</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Mechanical ventilation is recommended due to paradoxical chest wall movement</cite>.
- Multimodal analgesia: initiate TEA early; escalate opioids cautiously; add acetaminophen, local infiltration, and nerve blocks; monitor for opioid-induced respiratory depression and hypercapnia; consider regional catheters with patient-controlled steps under capnographic surveillance.<cite id="dace93ac-2">A review of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative considerations improves outcomes; neuraxial techniques central to pain</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Epidural anesthesia for postoperative pain relief reduces opioid needs</cite>.
- Early mobilization and respiratory therapy: incentive spirometry, mobilize as tolerated, and incorporate chest physiotherapy; for kyphoscoliosis, tailor mobilization to avoid pain precipitants and prevent VAP.<cite id="88bd2df5-8">Optimization postoperatively prevents atelectasis and secretion retention, facilitating early mobilization</cite>.

Special scenarios and syndromic comorbidity
- Poland syndrome: expect ipsilateral chest wall hypoplasia, paradoxical motion, and respiratory compromise; anticipate difficult airway, limited chest expansion, and possible need for bronchial intubation in severe cases; maintain vigilant hemodynamics and oxygenation; use regional anesthesia for pain sparing respiration and to reduce transfusion needs.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical chest movement requires mechanical ventilation and careful anesthetic management</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-1">Poland syndrome patients could face challenges due to thoracic deformities impairing ventilation; management requires tailored strategies</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Anaesthetic considerations for pectus repair apply broadly to patients with Poland syndrome and chest wall deformities</cite>.
- Non-REM neuromuscular disease: in limb-sparing procedures with chest wall involvement (e.g., myotonic dystrophy), titrate NM blockade conservatively; avoid deep prolonged block; screen for strabismus and diaphragmatic paralysis; maintain spontaneous ventilation if feasible.<cite id="dace93ac-6">Pectus-related anesthesia stresses neuromuscular management; careful intraoperative monitoring prevents respiratory sequelae</cite>.
- Dentures and elderly patients: remove dentures preoperatively; if not possible, increase field of view, suction, and backup airway; consider awake bronchoscopy; plan for longer recovery in elderly patients with baseline pulmonary disease.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Pectus repair commonly presents at the anesthesiologist with airway and respiratory concerns</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical breathing can jeopardize gas exchange, especially in elderly or denture-dependent patients</cite>.
- Upper-airway and tracheal anomalies with limb/chest procedures (e.g., thoracic inlet tumors, tracheal stents): obtain bronchial tree status and plan fiberoptic bronchoscopy access; avoid malpositioned tubes; coordinate with ENT/bronchoscopy team.<cite id="88bd2df5-1">Anesthetic management requires recognition of altered respiratory function and airway management strategies</cite>.

Practical perioperative checklists (summary)
- Airway: dentures off; difficult airway cart; fiberoptic/awake plan; cervical spine precautions; secure oxygenation first; consider bronchial intubation if paradoxical motion is severe.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">Failed intubation history in Poland syndrome necessitates alternative airway strategies</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical chest movement mandates mechanical ventilation</cite>.
- Breathing: high vigilance on SpO2, capnography, respiratory mechanics; prone/lateral recruitment; prone-safe intubation equipment; expect restrictive compliance.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Optimize oxygenation and V/Q mismatch; thoracic epidural reduces opioid depression of respiration</cite>.
- Circulation: anticipate tachycardic/hypotensive swings; load fluids; in ACHD, titrate inotropes and vasopressors; avoid excessive afterload during traction; maintain safe systolic ranges.<cite id="dace93ac-8">General anesthesia maintenance should support hemodynamics per standard anesthetic principles</cite>.
